You may mock the saints, but with God it is vastly different.
Therefore, I beg you, give up this practice.
Let us now speak of the two kinds.
Although I hold that it is necessary that the sacrament be received in both kinds, according to the Lord's institution, nevertheless it must not be made compulsory or a general law.
We must occupy ourselves with the Word, practice it and preach it.
For the result we should look entirely to the Word, and let everyone have his liberty in this matter.
Where that is not done, the sacrament becomes an outward observance and a hypocrisy, which is just what the devil wants.
But when the Word is given free course and is not bound to any observance, it takes hold of one person today and falls into his heart; tomorrow it touches another, and so on.
So it will do its work quietly and soberly, and no one will know how it all came about.
I was glad when someone wrote to me that some people in this city had begun to receive the sacrament in both kinds.
You should have let it remain so and not have forced it into a law.
But now you go at it pell-mell, and headlong force everyone into it.
Dear friends, you will not succeed that way.
And if you want to be regarded as better Christians than others because you take the sacrament into your hands and receive it in both kinds, you are really poor Christians indeed!
In this way even a sow could be a Christian, for she has a big enough snout to receive the sacrament outwardly.
We must deal soberly with such high things.
Dear friends, this must be no mockery, and if you would listen to me, give it up.
If you will not listen to me, no one needs to drive me away from you—I will leave you unbidden, and I shall regret that I ever preached so much as one sermon in this place.

The other things could be passed over, but this cannot be passed over; you have gone so far that people say: "At Wittenberg there are very good Christians, for they take the sacrament with their hands and handle the cup, and then they go to their brandy and drink until they are drunk."
In this way the weak and simple-minded are driven away, who would come to us if as much instruction had been given to them as was given to us.
But if there is anyone so stupid that he must touch the sacrament with his hands, let him have it brought home to his house and there let him handle it to his heart's content.

But in public let him abstain, since that will do him no harm, and the offense will be avoided that is caused to our brothers, sisters and neighbors, who are now so angry with us that they are ready to kill us.
I may say that none of the enemies who have opposed me until now have brought so much grief upon me as you have.
This is enough for today; we shall continue tomorrow.
In our discussion of the chief things we have come to the reception of the sacrament, which we have not yet finished.
Today we shall see how we must conduct ourselves here, and also who is worthy to receive the sacrament and who belongs there.
It is very necessary here that your hearts and consciences be well instructed, so that you distinguish well between the outward reception and the inner, spiritual reception.
This is the bodily and outward reception: when a man receives the body of Christ and His blood with his mouth.
Anyone can receive the sacrament in this way, for such reception may be without faith and love.
But that reception does not make a man a Christian, for if it did, even a mouse would be a Christian, for it too can eat the bread and drink out of the cup.
It is such a simple thing to do.
But the true, inner, spiritual reception is a very different thing, for it consists in the right use of the sacrament and of its fruits.
I would say in the first place that such reception is the true inner one, and is a reception in faith.
We Christians have no other outward sign by which we may be distinguished from others than this sacrament and baptism; but a mere outward reception, without faith, amounts to nothing.
There must be faith to make one well prepared for the reception and acceptable before God; otherwise it is all sham and mere outward show, which is not Christianity at all.
Christianity is a matter of faith, which is never bound to any outward work.

But faith (which we all must have if we wish to go to the sacrament worthily) is a firm trust that Christ, the Son of God, stands in our place and has taken all our sins upon His shoulders, that He is the eternal satisfaction for our sin and reconciles us with God the Father.
He who has this faith belongs to this sacrament, and neither devil nor hell nor sin can harm him.
Do you ask why?
Because God is his protector and defender.
And when I have this faith, then I am certain that God is fighting for me; I can defy devil, death, hell and sin, and all the harm with which they threaten me.
This is the great, priceless treasure given us in Christ, which human words cannot describe.
Only faith can take hold of the heart, and not everyone has such faith.

Therefore this sacrament must not be made a law, as the most holy father, the pope, has done with his fools' commandment: All Christians must go to the sacrament at holy Eastertide, and whoever does not go shall not be buried in consecrated ground.
Is it not a foolish law that the pope has set up?
You ask why? Because we are not all alike; we do not all have equal faith; the faith of one is stronger than that of another.
It is therefore impossible for the sacrament to be made a law, and the greatest sins are committed at Easter solely because of this unchristian command, which would drive everybody to the sacrament.
And if all robbery, usury, unchastity and all the other sins were thrown onto one great heap, this sin would tower above it—even at the time and place of seemingly greatest silliness.
And why? Because the pope can look into no one's heart to see whether he has faith or not.

But if you believe that God is with you and stakes all His treasures and His blood for you, as if He said: Fall in behind Me without fear or delay, and then let come what may to try to harm you; let devil, death, sin and hell and all creation try it; I shall go before you, for I will be your captain and your shield; trust Me and rely on Me completely—he who believes this way cannot be harmed by devil, hell, sin or death; if God fights for him, what can you do to him?
He who has such faith is fit for the altar and receives the sacrament as an assurance, or seal, or sign to assure him of God's promises and grace.
But such faith we do not all have; would to God one-tenth of Christians had it!

See, such rich, immeasurable treasures, which God in His grace showers upon us, cannot be the possession of everyone, but only of those who suffer either bodily or spiritual adversity: the bodily through the persecution of men, and the spiritual through despair of conscience; outwardly or inwardly, when the devil makes your heart weak, timid and discouraged, so that you do not know how you stand with God, and when he reproaches you with your sins.
And in such terrified and trembling hearts alone God desires to dwell, as the prophet Isaiah says [Isa. 66:2].

For he who has not felt the battle within him, is not distressed by his sins nor has a daily quarrel with them, and wishes for no protector, defender and shield to stand before him, is not yet ready for this food.
This food demands a hungering and longing man, for it delights to enter a hungering soul, one that is in constant battle with its sins and eager to be rid of them.
He who is not prepared in this way should abstain from this sacrament for a while, for this food is not for a satisfied and full heart, and if it comes to such a heart, it is harmful.

Therefore, if we think about and feel within us such distress of conscience and the fear of a timid heart, we shall come with all humility and reverence, and not rush to it pell-mell, with insolence and without fear and humility.
We are not always fit for it; today I have the grace and am fit for it, but not tomorrow; indeed, it may be that for six months I have no desire or fitness for it.

Therefore those are the most worthy who are constantly troubled by death and the devil, and they receive it most fittingly, to remind them and strengthen them in the faith that no harm can come to them, for He is now with them, from Whom no one can take them away; let death or devil or sin come, they cannot harm them.
This is what Christ did when He prepared to institute the blessed sacrament.

He brought anguish upon His disciples and trembling to their hearts when He said that He would go away from them [Matt. 26:2], and again they were tormented when He said: One of you shall betray Me [Matt. 26:21].
Do you not think that cut them to the heart?
Truly, they received the word with all fear, and sat there as though they were all traitors to God.
And only after He had made them all tremble with fear and sorrow did He institute the blessed sacrament as a comfort, and consoled them again.
For this bread is a comfort for the sorrowing, a healing for the sick, a life for the dying, a food for all the hungry, and a rich treasure for all the poor and needy.
Let this be enough for now concerning the proper use of this sacrament.
I commend you to God.

Yesterday we heard about the use of the holy and blessed sacrament and saw who are worthy to receive it: those in whom is the fear of death, who have timid and despairing consciences and who live in fear of hell.
All such come prepared to partake of this food for the strengthening of their weak faith and the comforting of their conscience.
This is the true and right use of this sacrament, and whoever does not find himself in this state, let him refrain from coming until God also takes hold of him and draws him through His Word.
We shall now speak of the fruit of this sacrament, which is love; that is, that we should treat our neighbor just as God has treated us.

Now we have received from God nothing but love and favor, for Christ has pledged and given us His righteousness and everything that He has, and has poured out upon us all His treasures, which no man can measure and no angel can understand or fathom, for God is a glowing furnace of love, reaching even from the earth to the heavens.
Love, I say, is a fruit of this sacrament.
But I do not yet see it among you here in Wittenberg, although there is much preaching of love and you ought to practice it above all other things.
This is the principal thing, and it alone is fitting for a Christian.
But no one shows eagerness for this, and you want to do all sorts of unnecessary things, which are of no account.

If you do not want to show yourselves Christians by your love, then leave the other things undone too, for St. Paul says in 1 Corinthians, "If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and do not have love, I am like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal."
[1 Cor. 13:1] This is a terrible saying of Paul's.

And further: "And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all the mysteries of God, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could move mountains, and do not have love, I am nothing.
And if I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing."
[1 Cor. 13:2–3] You have not got as far as that, although you have received great and rich gifts from God, especially a knowledge of the Scriptures.
It is true, you have the pure Gospel and the true Word of God, but no one as yet has given his goods to the poor, no one has yet been burned, and even these things would profit nothing without love.
You would take all of God's goods in the sacrament, and yet not pour them out again in love.

No one will lend another a helping hand, no one thinks first of another, but everyone looks out for himself and his own gain, seeks only his own and lets everything else go as it will—if anybody is helped, well and good.
No one looks after the poor or seeks how to help them.
It is pitiful. You have heard many sermons about it, and all my books are full of it and have the one purpose, to urge you to faith and love.
And if you will not love one another, God will send a great plague upon you; let this be a warning to you, for God will not reveal His Word and have it preached in vain.
You are tempting God too far, my friends.
If someone in times past had preached the Word to our forefathers, they would perhaps have acted differently.
Or if the Word were preached today to many poor children in the cloisters, they would receive it with much greater joy than you.
You do not heed it at all, and give yourselves to other things, which are unnecessary and foolish.
I commend you to God.

chapters.title: The Eighth Sermon: A Short Summary of the Sermon of Dr. M. Luther Delivered on Reminiscere Sunday on Private Confession

s: Now we have heard all the things that ought to be considered here, except confession.
Of this we shall speak now.
In the first place, there is a confession which is founded on the Scriptures; namely, when someone commits a sin publicly, or with other people's knowledge, and is accused before the congregation.
If he abandons his sin, they intercede for him with God.
But if he will not listen to the congregation, he is excluded from the church and cast out, so that no one will have anything to do with him.
And this confession is commanded by God in Matthew 18: "If your brother trespasses against you (so that you and others are offended), go and tell him his fault, just between you and him alone."
[Matt. 18:15] Of this confession there is no longer even a trace to be found, and in this respect the Gospel is set aside in this place.
Whoever could reestablish it would perform a good work.
Here is where you ought to have taken pains and reestablished this kind of confession, and let the other things go.
For by this no one would have been offended, and it would have been accomplished without disturbance.
It should be done in this way: When you see a usurer, adulterer, thief or drunkard, you should go to him in secret and admonish him to give up his sin.
If he will not listen, you should take two others with you and admonish him once more, in a brotherly way, to give up his sin.

But if he scorns that, you should tell the pastor before the whole congregation, have your witnesses with you, and accuse him before the pastor in the presence of the people, saying: "Dear pastor, this man has done this and that, and would not receive our brotherly admonition to give up his sin.
Therefore I accuse him, together with my witnesses who were present."

And then, if he will not give up and willingly acknowledge his guilt, the pastor should exclude him and put him under the ban before the whole assembly, for the sake of the congregation, until he comes to himself and is received back again.
This would be Christian.
But I cannot undertake to carry it out single-handedly.
Secondly, a confession is necessary for us when we go away into a corner by ourselves, and confess to God Himself and pour out all our faults before Him.
And this confession is also commanded.
From this comes the familiar word of Scripture: "Facite judicium et justitiam" (Do judgment and righteousness).

[Gen. 18:19] Judicium facere est nos ipsos accusare et damnare; justitiam autem facere est fidere misericordiae Dei (To do judgment is to accuse and condemn ourselves; but to do righteousness is to trust in the mercy of God).
As it is written, "Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times."
[Ps. 106:3] The judgment is nothing else than a man's knowing and judging and condemning himself, and this is true humility and self-abasement.
The righteousness is nothing else than a man's knowing himself and praying to God for the mercy and help through which God raises him up again.

This is what David means when he says: "I have sinned; I will confess my transgressions to the Lord" [Ps. 32:5f.], and, "You forgave the iniquity of my sin; for this all Your saints shall pray to You."
Thirdly, there is also a confession when one takes another aside and tells him what troubles him, so that he may hear a word of comfort from him; and this confession is commanded by the pope.
It is this urging and forcing that I condemned when I wrote concerning confession, and I refuse to go to confession simply because the pope wishes it and has commanded it.
For I want him to keep his hands off confession and not make of it a compulsion or command, which he does not have the power to do.
Yet I will let no one take private confession away from me, and I would not give it up for all the treasures in the world, since I know what comfort and strength it has given me.
No one knows what it can do for him except one who has struggled much with the devil.
Indeed, the devil would have slain me long ago if confession had not sustained me.
For there are many doubts that a man cannot resolve by himself, and so he takes a brother aside and tells him his trouble.

What harm is there if he humbles himself a little before his neighbor, puts himself to shame, looks for a word of comfort from him, and takes it to himself and believes it, as if he heard it from God Himself, as we read in Matthew 18: "If two of you agree concerning anything that they ask, it shall be done for them"? [Matt. 18:19]
And we must have many absolutions, so that we may strengthen our timid consciences and despairing hearts against the devil and against God.
Therefore no one shall forbid confession, nor keep or drive anyone away from it.

And if anyone wrestles with his sins, is eager to be rid of them and looks for some assurance from the Scriptures, let him go and confess to another in secret, and receive what is said to him there as if it came directly from God's own lips.
Whoever has the strong and firm faith that his sins are forgiven may pass over this confession and confess to God alone.
But how many have such a strong faith?
Therefore, as I have said, I will not let this private confession be taken from me.
Yet I would force no one to it, but leave the matter to everyone's free will.

For our God is not so miserly that He has left us with only one comfort or strengthening for our conscience, or only one absolution; rather, we have many absolutions in the Gospel, and are richly showered with them.
For instance, we have this in the Gospel: "If you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you."
[Matt. 6:14] Another comfort we have in the Lord's Prayer: "Forgive us our trespasses" [Matt. 6:12], etc.
A third is our baptism, when I reason like this: See, my Lord, I am baptized in Your name so that I may be assured of Your grace and mercy.
After that we have private confession, when I go and receive a sure absolution as if God Himself spoke it, so that I may be assured that my sins are forgiven.

Finally I take the blessed sacrament for myself, when I eat His body and drink His blood as a sign that I am rid of my sins and that God has freed me from all my frailties; and in order to make me sure of this, He gives me His body to eat and His blood to drink, so that I shall not and cannot despair: I cannot doubt that I have a gracious God.
So we see that confession must not be despised, but that it is a true comfort.

And since we need many absolutions and comforts, because we must fight against the devil, death, hell and sin, we must not allow any of our weapons to be taken away, but must keep intact the whole armor and equipment that God has given us for use against our enemies.
For you do not yet know what work it is to fight with the devil and to overcome him.
I know it well; I have eaten salt with him once or twice.
I know him well, and he knows me well, too.
If only you knew him, you would not drive out confession in this way.
I commend you to God. Amen.
Text: Romans 12:16-21.
16 Do not be wise in your own opinions.
17 Repay no one evil for evil.
Take thought for what is honorable in the sight of all men.
18 If it is possible, as far as it lies in you, be at peace with all men.
19 Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to the wrath of God; for it is written, Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.
20 But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by doing so you will heap coals of fire on his head.
21 Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
"Do not be wise in your own opinions."
64. The lesson as it is read in the Church ends here.
We will therefore note the remaining portion only briefly.

"Your own opinions," as used here, means the stubborn attitude toward temporal things held by the person who is unwilling to be taught, who himself knows best in everything, who yields to no one, and who calls good whatever agrees with his own ideas.
The Christian should be more willing to give way in temporal affairs.
Let him not be quarrelsome, but rather yielding, since the Word of God and faith are not involved; it is only a question of personal honor, of friends, and of worldly things.
"Repay no one evil for evil."
65. In the counsel above (verse 14) to "curse not," the writer of the epistle has in mind those who are unable to avenge themselves or to return evil for evil.
These have no other option but to curse, to call down evil upon their oppressors.
Here, however, the reference is to those who have equal power to repay one another evil for evil, malice for malice, whether by things done or things left undone—and usually they are left undone.
But the Christian should return good for evil, and not leave it undone.
God lets his sun shine on the evil and on the good.
Matthew 5:45.
"Take thought for what is honorable in the sight of all men."

66. This command is similar to the one he gives the Thessalonians (1 Thess 5:22), "Abstain from every appearance of evil"; and the Philippians (ch. 4:8): "Whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report; if there is any virtue, and if there is any praise, think on these things."
The reference is purely to our outward conduct.
Paul would not have the Christian think himself free to do as he pleases, regardless of whether others approve.
Only in the things of faith does the Christian have that privilege.

His outward conduct should be beyond reproach, acceptable to all men; in keeping with the teaching of First Corinthians 10:32-33, to please all men, giving offense neither to Jews nor to Gentiles; and obedient to Peter's advice (1 Pet 2:12), "Keep your behavior proper among the Gentiles."
"If it is possible, as far as it lies in you, be at peace with all men."
67. Outward peace among people is meant here—peace with Christians and heathen, with the godly and the wicked, the high and the low.
We must give no occasion for strife; rather, we are to endure every ill patiently, never allowing peace to be disturbed on our account.
We must not return evil for evil, blow for blow; for whoever does so gives rise to contention.
Paul adds, "As far as it lies in you."
We are to avoid injuring anyone, so that we are not the ones who cause contention.
We must show friendliness to all men, even though they are not friendly to us.
It is impossible to keep peace at all times.
The saying goes, "I can live in peace only as long as my neighbor is willing."
But it is in our power to leave others in peace, friends and foes, and to endure the contentions of all.
"Oh yes," you say, "but where would we be then?" Listen:
"Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to the wrath of God: for it is written, Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord."
68. Note that in forbidding us to return blow for blow and to resort to vengeance, the apostle implies that our enjoyment of peace depends on our quietly enduring the disturbance caused by others.
He not only assures us that we will be avenged, but he also frightens us away from usurping the office of God, to whom alone vengeance and retribution belong.

Indeed, he rather laments the fate of the Christian's enemies, who expose themselves to God's wrath; he would move us to pity them, seeing that we must give place to wrath and let them fall into the hands of God.

The vengeance and wrath of God are dealt out in various ways: through the instrument of the political government; at the hands of the devil; by illness, hunger, and pestilence; by fire and water; by war, hostility, and disgrace; and by every possible kind of misfortune on earth.
Every creature may serve as the rod and the weapon of God when he intends to chastise.
As it says in the Wisdom of Solomon 5:17: "He shall ... make the creature his weapon for vengeance on his enemies."
69. So Paul says, "Give place to wrath."
I have inserted the words "of God" to make the meaning of the text clearer; the wrath of God is meant, and not the wrath of man.
The thought is not of giving place to the anger of our enemies.
True, there may be occasion even for that, but Paul is not referring here to man's anger.
Evidently he means misfortunes and plagues, which are regarded as expressions of God's wrath.
Possibly the apostle left out the phrase to avoid giving the idea that only the final wrath of God is meant—his anger on the last day, when he will inflict punishment without any instrument.
Paul would include here all wrath, whether temporal or eternal, to which God gives expression in his chastisements.
This is an Old Testament way of speaking.
Phinehas says (Josh 22:18), "Tomorrow he will be angry with ...
Israel." And Moses in several places speaks of God's anger being kindled.
See Numbers 11:1, 10, 33.

I mention these things in order to teach that when the political government wields the sword of punishment against its enemies, it should be regarded as an expression of God's wrath; and that the statement in Deuteronomy 32:35, "Vengeance is mine," does not refer only to punishment inflicted by God directly, without any instrument.
"But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by doing so you will heap coals of fire on his head."
70. This teaching confirms what I have already said—that the Christian's enemies are to be pitied because they are subject to the wrath of God.
Therefore it is not Christian to injure them; rather, we should do them favors.
Paul here introduces a quotation from Solomon.
Proverbs 25:21-22. Heaping coals of fire on the head, in my view, means doing favors for the enemy.
Set aflame by our kindness, he eventually becomes displeased with himself and more kindly disposed toward us.
Coals here are benefits, or favors.
The coals in the censer likewise stand for the favors, or blessings, of God; they are a figure of our prayers, which should rise with fervor.

Some say that the coals represent the Law and judgments of God (see Psalm 18:8, "Coals were kindled by it"), reasoning that as a result of the Christian's favors, his enemy is compelled to censure himself and to feel the weight of God's Law and his judgments.
I do not think a Christian should desire punishment to fall on his enemy, though such an explanation of the sentence is not unfitting.
In fact, it rather agrees with the command, "Give place to wrath"; that is, do good, and then wrath—the coals—will readily fall on the enemy.
"Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good."
71. With this concluding counsel, it seems to me, Paul himself explains the phrase "coals of fire" in keeping with the first idea—that the malice of an enemy is to be overcome with good.
Overcoming by force is the same as lending yourself to evil and wronging the enemy who wrongs you.
By such a course your enemy overcomes you, and you are made evil like him.
But if you overcome him with good, he will be made righteous like you.
A spiritual overcoming is meant here; the disposition, the heart, the soul—yes, the devil who stirs up the evil—are overcome.
Text: Romans 13:8-10.
8 Owe nothing to anyone, except to love one another; for he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.

9 For this, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not kill, You shall not steal, You shall not covet, and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word, namely, You shall love your neighbor as yourself.
10 Love works no ill to its neighbor; love, therefore, is the fulfillment of the law.
1. This lesson, like the two preceding epistle lessons, is one of admonition, and directs our attention to the fruits of faith.
Here, however, Paul briefly sums up all the fruits of faith in love.
In the preceding verses he enjoined submission to temporal government—the rendering of tribute, custom, fear and honor wherever due—since all governmental power is ordained by God.
Then follows our lesson: “Owe nothing to anyone,” and so on.
2. I shall pass over the various explanations usually invented for this command, “Owe nothing to anyone, except to love one another.”
To me it means, clearly and simply: not as men, but as Christians, are we under obligation.
Our indebtedness should be the free obligation of love.
It should not be compulsory and prescribed by law.
Paul holds up two forms of obligation: one is inspired by law, the other by love.
Legal obligations make us debtors to men; an example is when one person has a claim against another for a debt.
The duties and tribute, the obedience and honor, that we owe to political government are of this legal kind.

Though in themselves these things are not essential to the Christian—they do not justify him or make him more righteous—yet, because he must live here on earth, he is under obligation, so far as outward conduct is concerned, to place himself on a level with other men in these things, and in general to help maintain temporal order and peace.
Christ paid the tribute money as a debt (Matthew 17:27), even though he had told Peter that he was under no obligation to do so and would have committed no sin before God by leaving it undone.
3. Another obligation is love, when a Christian voluntarily makes himself a servant of all men.
Paul says (1 Corinthians 9:19), “For though I was free from all men, I brought myself into bondage to all.”
This is not a requirement of human laws; no one who fails in this duty is censured or punished for neglect of legal obligations.
The world knows nothing of the commandment to love—of the obligation to submit to and serve a fellow man.
This fact is very evident.

Let a man be wealthy, and so long as he refrains from dishonoring his neighbor’s wife, from taking his neighbor’s goods, from staining his honor or injuring his person, he is righteous in the eyes of the law.
No law punishes him for greed and stinginess; for refusing to lend, to give, to aid, and to help his wronged neighbor obtain justice.
Laws made to restrain the outward man are directed only against evil works, which they forbid and punish.
Good works are left to voluntary performance.
Civil law does not extort them by threats and punishment, but commends and rewards them, as the Law of Moses also does.
4. Paul would teach Christians so to conduct themselves toward men and civil authority as to give no occasion for complaint or censure on account of any unpaid debt to temporal law.
He would not have them fail to satisfy the claims of legal obligation, but rather go beyond its requirements, making themselves debtors voluntarily and serving those who have no claim on them.
On this subject Paul says (Romans 1:14), “I am a debtor both to Greeks and to Barbarians.”
Love’s obligation enables a man to do more than is actually required of him.
Hence the Christian always willingly renders to the state and to the individual every service demanded by temporal regulations, allowing no claims against himself in this respect.
5. Paul’s injunction, then, might be expressed thus: Owe all men, that you may owe none; owe everything, that you may owe nothing.
This sounds paradoxical. But the one indebtedness is that of love, an obligation to God.
The other is indebtedness to temporal law, an obligation in the eyes of the world.
He who makes himself a servant, who takes upon himself love’s obligation to all men, goes so far that no one dares complain of any omission; indeed, he goes farther than anyone could desire.
Thus he is made free.
He lives under obligation to no one by the very fact that he puts himself under obligation to all.
This manner of presenting the thought would be upheld by the Spirit in connection with other duties as well; for instance: Do no good work, that you may do only good works.
Never be pious and holy, if you would always be pious and holy.

As Paul says (Romans 12:16), “Do not be wise in your own conceits”; or (1 Corinthians 3:18), “If any man among you thinks that he is wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may become wise.”
It is in this sense that we say: Owe all men, that you may owe no man; or, “Owe nothing to anyone, except to love one another.”
6. Such counsel is given with the two obligations in mind.
He who would do works truly good in the sight of God must guard against works that seem brilliant in the eyes of the world, works by which men presume to become righteous.
He who desires to be righteous and holy must guard against the holiness attained by works without faith.
Again, the seeker after wisdom must reject the wisdom of men, of nature—wisdom apart from the Spirit.
In the same way, he who would be under obligation to none must obligate himself to all in every respect.
By so doing, he retains no claim of his own.
Consequently, he soon rises above all law, for law binds only those who have claims of their own.
Rightly is it said, “Qui cedit omnibus bonis, omnibus satisfecit,” “He who surrenders all his property satisfies all men.”
How can one be under obligation when he does not, and cannot, possess anything?
It is love’s way to give all.
The best way, then, to be under obligation to none is, through love, to obligate oneself in every respect to all men.

In this sense it may be said: If you would live, die; if you would not be imprisoned, imprison yourself; if you do not wish to go to hell, descend there; if you object to being a sinner, be a sinner; if you would escape the cross, take it upon yourself; if you would conquer the devil, let him vanquish you; would you overcome a wicked person, allow him to overcome you.
The meaning of it all is that we should readily submit to God, to the devil and to men, and willingly allow them their pleasure; we are to insist on nothing, but accept all things as they come.
This is why Paul speaks as he does, “Owe nothing to anyone,” and so on, instead of letting the matter rest with the preceding injunction in verse 5, “Render therefore to all their due,” and so on.

blocks.x: Love Fulfills the Law.

s: “For he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.”
7. Since we have often spoken of the character and fruits of love, it is unnecessary to take up the subject here.
The topic is sufficiently treated in the epistle lesson for the Sunday before Lent.
We will look at the command to love as it stands in the Law of God.
Innumerable, endless, are the books and teachings produced for the direction of man’s conduct.
And still there is no limit to the making of books and laws.
Note the ecclesiastical and civil regulations, the spiritual orders and stations.

These laws and teachings might be tolerated, might be received with more favor, if they were founded upon and administered according to the one great law—the one rule or measure—of love; as the Scriptures do, which present many different laws, but all born of love, and comprehended in and subject to it.
And these laws must give way, must become invalid, when they conflict with love.
Of Love’s higher authority we find many illustrations in the Scriptures.
Christ makes particular mention of the matter in Matthew 12:3-4, where David and his companions ate the holy showbread.
Though a certain law forbade anyone but the priests to eat this holy food, Love was empress here, and free.
Love was over the Law, making it subject to herself.
The Law had to give way for the time being, had to become invalid, when David suffered hunger.
The Law had to submit to the sentence: “David is hungry and must be relieved, for Love commands, Do good to your needy neighbor.
Yield, therefore, you Law.
Do not prevent the accomplishment of this good.
Rather, accomplish it yourself.
Serve him in his need.
Do not interpose your prohibitions.”
In connection with this same incident, Christ teaches that we are to do good to our neighbor on the Sabbath, and to minister as necessity demands, whatever the Sabbath restrictions of the Law.
For when a brother’s need calls, Love is authority and the Law of the Sabbath is void.
8. If laws were conceived and administered in love, the number of laws would matter little.
Though one might not hear or learn all of them, he would learn, from the one or two he knew, the principle of love taught in all.
And though he were to know all laws, he might not discover the principle of love any more readily than he would in one.

Paul teaches this method of understanding and mastering law when he says: “Owe nothing to anyone, except to love one another”; “He who loves another has fulfilled the law”; “If there is any other commandment, it is briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, You shall love your neighbor as yourself”; “Love works no ill to its neighbor”; “Love is the fulfilling of the law.”
Every word in this epistle lesson proves Love the mistress of all law.
9. Further, no greater calamity, wrong and misery is possible on earth than the teaching and enforcing of laws without love.

In such a case, laws are nothing but a ruinous curse, proving true the proverbs, “summum jus, summa injustitia,” “The strictest right is the greatest wrong”; and again, Solomon’s words (Ecclesiastes 7:17), “Noli nimium esse justus,” “Do not be righteous to excess.”
Here is where we leave unnoticed the beam in our own eye and proceed to remove the speck from our neighbor’s eye.
Laws without love make the conscience timid and fill it with unreasonable terror and despair, to the great injury of body and soul.
Thus much trouble and labor are spent, all to no purpose.
10. An illustration in point is the incident of David in his hunger, mentioned before.
1 Samuel 21:6.

Had the priest been disposed to refuse David the holy bread, had he blindly insisted on honoring the prohibitions of the Law and failed to perceive the authority of Love, had he denied this food to him who was hungry, what would have been the result?
As far as the priest’s help went, David would have had to perish of hunger, and the priest would have been guilty of murder for the sake of the Law.
Here, indeed, “summum jus, summa injustitia”—the strictest right would have been the greatest wrong.

Moreover, on examining the heart of a priest who would be so foolish, you would find there the extreme abomination of making sin where there is no sin, and a matter of conscience where there is no occasion for it.
For he holds it a sin to eat the bread, when in reality it is an act of love and righteousness.
Then, too, he regards his act of murder—letting David die of hunger—not as a sin, but as a good work and a service to God.
11. But who can fully portray this blind, perverted, abominable folly?
It is the committing of an evil that the devil himself cannot outdo.
For it makes sin where there is no sin, and a matter of conscience without cause.
It robs men of grace, salvation, virtue, and God with all his blessings, and that without reason, falsely and deceitfully.
It emphatically denies and condemns God.
Again, it makes murder and injustice a good work, a divine service.
It puts the devil with his falsehoods in the place of God.
It establishes the worst form of idolatry and ruins body and soul, destroying the former by hunger and the latter by a terrified conscience.
It makes God into the devil, and the devil into God.
It makes hell of heaven and heaven of hell; righteousness of sin, and sin of righteousness.
This I call perversion—where the strictest justice is the greatest wrong.
To this depravity Ezekiel refers (13:18-19): “Thus says the Lord Jehovah: Woe to the women who sew pillows upon all elbows, and make kerchiefs for the heads of persons of every stature to hunt souls!
Will you hunt down the souls of my people, and preserve souls alive for yourselves?

And you have profaned me among my people for handfuls of barley and for pieces of bread, to slay the souls that should not die, and to preserve alive the souls that should not live, through your lies told to my people, who give ear to lies.”

What does this mean but that the blind teachers of the Law terrify the conscience, and put sin and death in the place of grace and life, and grace and life where there is only sin and death; and all for a handful of barley and a bit of bread?

In other words, such teachers devote themselves to laws concerning strictly external matters, things that perish with the using, such as a drink of water and a morsel of bread, wholly neglecting love and harassing the conscience with fear of sin leading to eternal death; as Ezekiel goes on to say (verses 22-23): “Because with lies you have grieved the heart of the righteous, whom I have not made sad, and strengthened the hands of the wicked, so that he should not turn back from his wicked way and be saved alive; therefore you shall no more see false visions, nor practice divinations; and I will deliver my people out of your hand; and you shall know that I am Jehovah.”

12. Mark this: it is making the hearts of the righteous sad to load them with sins when their works are good; it is strengthening the hands of the wicked to make their works good when they are nothing but sin.
On this subject we read (Psalm 14:5): “There they were in great fear; for God is among the generation of the righteous.”
That is, the sting of conscience fills them with fear where there is no reason either for fear or for a troubled conscience.
What is really noble service to God is feared as sin.

The thought of the last passage is: when they ought to call upon God and serve him, they fear such conduct is sin and not divine service; again, when they have reason to fear a service that is not divine, they are secure and unafraid.
Isaiah’s words (29:13) are to the same effect: “Their fear of me is a commandment of men which has been taught them.”
The perverted people spoken of always corrupt everything.
They confidently call on God where there is only the devil; they fearfully refrain from calling on God where God is.
13. Such, note well, is the wretched condition of those who are blindly occupied with laws and works and fail to grasp the purpose of law and its mistress, Love.
Note, also, in the case of our miserable churchmen and their followers, how rigidly they cling to their own inventions!
Though all the world come to ruin, their devices must be upheld; they must be perpetuated regardless of bodily sickness and death, or of suffering and ruin for the soul.
They even regard such destruction and ruin as divine service, and know no fear or remorse of conscience.
Indeed, so firmly entrenched are they in their wickedness that they will never turn back from it.

Moreover, should one of their wretched number be permitted to relieve the distress of his body and soul—to eat meat, to marry—he is afraid, he feels remorse of conscience; he is uncertain about sin and law, about death and hell; he does not call on God, nor serve him; all this, even though the body should die ten deaths and the soul go to the devil a hundred times.

14. Observe, then, the state of the world; how little flesh and blood can accomplish even in their best efforts; how dangerous it is to undertake to rule by law alone—indeed, how impossible it is, without great danger, to govern and instruct souls with mere laws, ignoring love and the Spirit, in whose hands lies the full power of all law.
It is written (Deuteronomy 33:2), “At his right hand was a fiery law for them.”
This is the law of love in the Spirit.
It shall govern all the laws at the left hand; that is, the external laws of the world.

It is said (Exodus 28:30) that the priest must wear upon his breast, in the breastplate, “the Urim and the Thummim”; that is, Light and Perfection, signifying the priest’s office to illuminate the Law—to give its true sense—and to keep and teach it faultlessly.
15. In the framing, the establishment and the observance of all laws, the aim should be, not the furtherance of the laws in themselves, not the advancement of works, but the exercise of love.
That is the true purpose of law, according to Paul here: “He who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.”
Therefore, when the law contributes to the injury rather than the benefit of our neighbor, it should be disregarded.
The same law may at one time benefit our neighbor and at another time injure him.
Consequently, it should be regulated according to its benefit to him.
Law should be made to serve in the same way that food and clothing and the other necessities of life serve.
We consider not the food and clothing in themselves, but their benefit to our needy neighbor.
And we stop dispensing them as soon as we see that they no longer add to his comfort.

16. Suppose you were to come across a man foolish enough to act with no other thought than that food and clothing are truly good things, and so proceed to stuff a needy person with unlimited food and drink until he chokes, and to clothe him until he suffocates, and then not to stop.

Suppose that to the command, “Stop, you have suffocated him, you have already overfed and overclothed him, and it is all wasted effort now,” the foolish man should reply: “You heretic, would you forbid good works?
Food, drink and clothing are good things; therefore we must not stop dispensing them; we cannot do too much.”
And suppose he went on forcing food and clothing on the man.
Tell me, what would you think of such a man?
He is a fool beyond all foolishness; he is madder than madness itself.

But such is very nearly the character of our churchmen today, and of those who are so blind in the exercise of law as to act as if works were the only requirement, and to suffocate body and soul, being ignorant that the one purpose of law is to call forth the exercise of love.
They make works superior to love, and a maid superior to her mistress.
Such perversion prevails to an extent distressing to think of, not to mention hearing and seeing it, or, more than that, practicing and permitting it ourselves.
17. The commandment of love is not a long one; it is short.
It is one injunction, not many.
It is not even a commandment, and at the same time it is all commandments.
Brief, and a unit in itself, its meaning is easily grasped.
But in its exercise it is far-reaching, for it includes and regulates all commandments.
So far as works are enjoined, it is no commandment at all; it names no particular work.
Yet it represents all commandments, because properly the fulfillment of all commandments is the fulfillment of this one.
The commandment of love suspends every commandment, yet it perpetuates all.
Its whole purpose is that we may recognize no commandment, no work, except as love dictates.
18. Since life on earth apart from works is an impossibility, there must necessarily be various commandments involving works.
Yet Love is supreme over these requirements, dictating the omission or the performance of works according to its own best interests, and permitting no works opposed to itself.
To illustrate: a driver, holding the reins, guides team and wagon at will.

If he were content merely to hold the reins, regardless of whether or not the team followed the road, the entire outfit—team, wagon, reins and driver—would soon be wrecked; the driver would be lying drowned in a ditch or a pool, or would have his neck broken going over stumps and rocks.
But if he skillfully regulates the movement of the outfit according to the road, observing where it is safe and where unsafe, he will proceed securely because wisely.
Were he, in his self-conceit, to drive straight ahead, trying to make the road conform to the movement of the wagon at his pleasure, he would soon see how beautifully his plan would work.
19. So it is when men are governed by laws and works, and the laws are not regulated according to the people.
The case is that of the driver who would regulate the road by the movements of the wagon.
True, the road is often well suited to the straight course of the wagon.
But just as truly the road is, in certain places, crooked and uneven, and then the wagon must conform to the course and condition of the road.
Men must adapt themselves to laws and regulations wherever possible and where the laws are beneficial.
But where laws prove harmful to men’s interests, the laws must yield.
The ruler must wisely make allowance for love, suspending works and laws.
Hence philosophers say that prudence—or circumspection or discretion, as the churchmen put it—is the guide and regulator of all virtues.
20. We read in a book of the ancient fathers that on a certain occasion when they had assembled, the question was raised: which is really the noblest work?
Various answers were given.
One said prayer, another fasting; but St. Anthony was of the opinion that of all works and virtues, discretion is the best and surest way to heaven.
These, however, were but childish, unspiritual ideas concerning their own self-chosen works.
A Christian views the matter in quite a different light, and more judiciously.
He concludes that neither discretion nor rashness avails before God.
Only faith and love are of service with him.
But love is true discretion; love is the driver and the true discretion in righteous works.
It always looks to the good of the neighbor, to the betterment of his condition; just as the discretion of the world looks to the general welfare of the governed in the adjustment of political laws.
Let this suffice on this point.

21. But the question arises: How can love fulfill the Law when love is only one of the fruits of faith, and we have often said that only faith in Christ removes our sins, justifies us and satisfies all the demands of the Law?
How can we make the two claims agree?
Christ says, too (Matthew 7:12): “All things, therefore, whatever you wish that men would do to you, even so do also to them: for this is the law and the prophets.”
Thus he shows that love for one’s neighbor fulfills both the Law and the prophets.
Again, he says (Matthew 22:37-40): “You shall love the Lord your God ... your neighbor as yourself.
On these two the whole law hangs, and the prophets.”
Where, then, does Paul stand, who says (Romans 3:31): “Do we then render the law void through faith?
By no means: rather, we establish the law.”
Again (Romans 3:28): “We hold, therefore, that a man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law.”
And again (Romans 1:17), “The righteous shall live by faith.”
22. I reply: As we have often said, we must properly distinguish between faith and love.
Faith deals with the heart, and love with works.
Faith removes our sins, makes us acceptable, justifies us.
And once we are accepted and justified as to our person, love is given us in the Holy Spirit and we delight in doing good.
Now, it is the nature of the Law to attack our person and demand good works; and it will not cease to demand until it gains its point.
We cannot do good works apart from the Spirit and love.
The Law compels us to know ourselves with our imperfections, and to recognize that we must become altogether different people if we are to satisfy the Law.
The Law does not demand so much of the heart as of works; in fact, it demands nothing but works and ignores the heart.
It leaves the individual to discover, from the works required, that he must become an altogether different person.
But faith, when it comes, creates a nature capable of accomplishing the works the Law demands.
Thus the Law is fulfilled.
So Paul’s sayings on the subject are beautiful and fitting.
The Law demands works of us; it must be fulfilled by works.
Hence it cannot in every sense be said that faith fulfills the Law.
However, it prepares the way and enables us to fulfill it, for the Law demands not us, but our works.
The Law constrains us—teaches us that we must be changed before we can accomplish its works; it makes us aware of our inability as we are.
On the other hand, love and works do not change us and do not justify us.
We must be changed in person and justified before we can love and do good works.
Our love and our works are evidence of justification and of a change, since they are impossible until the individual is free from sin and made righteous.

23. This explanation is given to enable us to perceive the true nature of the Law, of faith and of love; to assign to each its own mission; and rightly to understand the declarations of Scripture in their harmonious relations: that while faith justifies, it does not fulfill the Law, and that while love does not justify, it does fulfill the Law.
The Law requires love and works, but does not mention the heart.
The heart is conscious of the Law, but love is not.

Just as the Law, in requiring works before faith exists, is a sign to the individual that leads him to recognize his utter lack of faith and righteousness and to conclude that he is conquered, so love, in its fulfillment of the Law after faith has come, is a sign and a proof to the individual of his faith and righteousness.
Law and love, then, bear witness to him concerning his unrighteousness or his righteousness.
After faith comes, love is evidence of righteousness.
Before faith, man feels the Law’s oppression because he knows he does not possess what the Law requires.
And the Law does not require a changed heart, but works.
Love and works do not bring about the fulfillment of the Law; they are themselves its fulfillment.
24. Now, though faith does not fulfill the Law, it contains that which brings about its fulfillment; it secures the Spirit and love by which the end is accomplished.
On the other hand, though love does not justify us, it makes manifest the faith by which we are justified.
Briefly, as Paul says here, “Love is the fulfillment of the law.”
His thought is: fulfillment of the Law is one thing, and effecting or supplying its fulfillment is another.
Love fulfills the Law in the sense that love itself is its fulfillment; but faith fulfills it in the sense that it supplies that by which it is fulfilled.
For faith loves and works, as is said in Galatians 5:6, “Faith works through love.”
The water fills the pitcher; so does the cupbearer.
The water fills of itself; the cupbearer fills with the water—“effective et formaliter implere,” as the sophists would say.
25. Faith is ever the doer, and love the deed.
The law requires the deed and thus forces the doer to be changed.
The Law is then fulfilled by the deed, which, however, the doer must perform.

Thus Paul rejects the fancies of the sophists, who in the matter of love would distinguish between the external work and the inner affection, saying: “Love is an inner affection that loves our neighbor when in our heart we wish him well.”
Its expression in works, however, they call the fruit of love.
But we will not discuss this idea.
Note that Paul calls love not only an affection, but an affectionate good deed.
Faith and the heart are the doer and fulfiller of the Law.
Paul says, “He who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.”
And love is the deed, the fulfilling; for he says, “Love is the fulfillment of the law.”
26. Another question arises: How can love for our neighbor be the fulfillment of the Law when we are required to love God supremely, even above our neighbor?
I reply: Christ answers the question when he tells us (Matthew 22:39) that the second commandment is like the first.
He makes love to God and love to our neighbor the same love.
The reason for this is, first: God, having no need of our works and benefactions for himself, bids us do for our neighbor what we would do for God.
For himself he asks only our faith and our acknowledgment of him as God.
The purpose of proclaiming his honor and rendering him praise and thanks here on earth is that our neighbor may be converted and brought into fellowship with God.
Such service is called the love of God, and is performed out of love to God; but it is exercised for the benefit of our neighbor only.

27. The second reason why God makes love to our neighbor an obligation equal to love to himself is this: God has made worldly wisdom foolish, desiring henceforth to be loved amid crosses and afflictions.

Paul says (1 Corinthians 1:21), “Seeing that in the wisdom of God the world through its wisdom did not come to know God, it was God’s good pleasure through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe.”
Therefore upon the cross he submitted himself to death and misery, and laid the same submission upon all his disciples.
Those who refused to love him before, when he bestowed on them food and drink, blessing and honor, must now love him in hunger and sorrow, in adversity and disgrace.
All works of love, then, must be directed to our wretched, needy neighbors.
In these lowly ones we are to find and love God, in them we are to serve and honor him, and only in this way can we do it.
The commandment to love God is wholly merged in that to love our neighbors.
28. These facts restrain those elusive, soaring spirits who seek after God only in great and glorious undertakings.
It stops the mouths of those who strive after greatness like his, who would force their way into heaven, presuming to serve and love him with their brilliant works.
But they miss him by passing him by in their earthly neighbor, in whom God would be loved and honored.
Therefore they will hear, on the last day, the sentence (Matthew 25:42), “I was hungry, and you did not give me to eat,” and so on.
For Christ laid aside his divinity and took upon himself the form of a servant for the very purpose of bringing down and centering upon our neighbor the love we extend to himself.
Yet we leave the Lord lying here in his humiliation while we gaze open-mouthed into heaven and make great pretensions of love and service to God.

blocks.x: All Commandments Summed Up in Love.

s: “For this, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not kill, You shall not steal, You shall not covet; and if there is any other commandment, it is briefly summed up in this word, namely, You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
29. Since love is the chief element of all law, it comprehends, as has been made sufficiently clear, all commandments.
Its one concern is to be useful to man and not harmful; therefore it readily finds the way.
Recognizing that man, out of his ardent self-love, seeks to promote his own interests and avoid injuring them, love endeavors to take the same course toward others.
We will consider the commandment just cited, noticing how ingeniously and wisely it is arranged.
It brings out four thoughts.
First, it states who is under obligation to love: you—the nearest, noblest, best individual we can command.
No one can fulfill the Law of God for another; each must do it for himself.
As Paul says (Galatians 6:5), “Each man shall bear his own burden.”

And (2 Corinthians 5:10): “For we must all be laid open before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive back the things done in the body, according to what he has done, be it good or bad.”
So it is said, “You, you yourself, must love”; not, “Let someone else love for you.”
Though one can and should pray that God may be gracious to another and help him, yet no one will be saved unless he himself fulfills God’s command.
It is not enough merely to pray that another may escape punishment, as the sellers of indulgences teach; much rather, we should pray that he may become righteous and keep God’s precepts.
30. Second, the commandment names the most noble virtue—love.
It does not say, “You shall feed your neighbor, give him drink, clothe him,” all of which are inestimably good works; it says, “You shall love him.”
Love is the chief virtue, the fountain of all virtues.
Love gives food and drink; it clothes, comforts, persuades, relieves and rescues.

What shall we say of it? For behold, he who loves gives himself, body and soul, property and honor, all his powers inner and outward, for the benefit of his needy neighbor, whether friend or enemy; he withholds nothing by which he may serve another.
There is no virtue like love; no special work can be assigned to it, as in the case of limited virtues such as chastity, mercy, patience, meekness and the like.
Love does all things.
It will suffer in life and in death, in every condition, and that even for its enemies.
Well may Paul say here that all other commandments are briefly comprehended in the injunction, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
31. Third, the commandment names, as the sphere of our love, the noblest field, the dearest friend—our neighbor.
It does not say, “You shall love the rich, the mighty, the learned, the saint.”
No, the unrestrained love set forth in this most perfect commandment does not divide itself among a few.
With it there is no respect of persons.
It is the nature of false, carnal, worldly love to have respect of persons, and to love only so long as it hopes to gain some profit.
When such hope ceases, that love also ceases.

The commandment of our text, however, requires of us free, spontaneous love to all men, whoever they may be, and whether friend or foe, a love that seeks no profit and ministers only what is beneficial.

Such love is most active and powerful in serving the poor, the needy, the sick, the wicked, the simple-minded and the hostile; among these it is always and under all circumstances necessary to suffer and endure, to serve and do good.
32. Note here that this commandment makes us all equal before God, without regard to the distinctions attaching to our stations in life, our persons, offices and occupations.

Since the commandment is to all—to every human being—a sovereign, if he is a human being, must confess the poorest beggar, the most wretched leper, to be his neighbor and his equal in the sight of God.
He is under obligation, according to this commandment, not to extend a measure of help, but to serve that neighbor with all he has and all he controls.
If he loves him as God here commands him to, he must give the beggar preference over his crown and all his realm; and if the beggar’s necessity requires it, he must give his life.
He is under obligation to love his neighbor, and must admit that such a person is his neighbor.
33. Is not this a superior, a noble commandment, which completely levels the most unequal individuals?

Is it not wonderfully comforting to the beggar to have servants and lovers of such honor? Is it not wonderful that his poverty commands the services of a king in his wealth? that to his sores and wounds are made subject the crown of wealth and the sweet fragrance of royal splendor?
But how strange it would seem to us to see kings and queens, princes and princesses, serving beggars and lepers, as we read that St. Elizabeth did!
Even this, however, would be a slight thing compared with what Christ has done.
No one can ever equal him in the obedience by which he has exalted this commandment.
He is a king whose honor surpasses that of all other kings; indeed, he is the Son of God.
And yet he puts himself on a level with the worst sinners, and serves them even to the point of dying for them.
Were ten kings of the earth to serve one beggar to the utmost, it would be a remarkable thing; but of what significance would it be in comparison with the service Christ has rendered?
The kings would be put to utter shame and would have to acknowledge that their service was unworthy of notice.
34. Learn, then, what condition the world is in—how far it is, not only from Christ’s immeasurable example, but from the commandment in this verse.

Where can anyone be found who understands the meaning of the little phrase “your neighbor,” even though there is, besides this commandment, the natural law of service written in the hearts of all men?

There is not one person who does not realize, and who is not forced to confess, the justice and truth of the natural law outlined in the command (Matthew 7:12), “All things therefore, whatever you would have men do to you, even so do you also to them.”
The light of this law shines in the reason that is inborn in all men.
If they would only heed it, what need would they have of books, teachers or laws?
They carry with them, in the depths of their hearts, a living book, able to teach them fully what to do and what to leave undone, what to accept and what to reject, and what decision to make.
Now, the command to love our neighbors as ourselves is equivalent to that other one, “Whatever you would have men do to you,” and so on.
Every individual desires to be loved and not hated; and he also feels and sees that he is obligated to show the same disposition toward others.
To carry out this obligation is to love another as himself.
But evil lust and sinful love obscure the light of the natural law and blind man, until he fails to perceive the guidebook in his heart and to follow the clear command of reason.
Hence he must be restrained and driven back by external laws and material books, with the sword and by force.
He must be reminded of his natural light, and his own heart must be revealed to him.
Yet admonition is of no avail; he does not see the light.
Evil lust and sinful love make him blind.
With the sword and with the laws of the state he must still be outwardly restrained from committing actual crimes.
35. The fourth thing the commandment sets before us is the standard by which we are to measure our love—an excellent model.
Those instructions and commandments are especially worthy which present examples.
This commandment holds up a truly living example—“yourself.”
It is a better model than any example the saints have given.
The saints are dead and their deeds are past, but this example is always alive.

Everyone must admit that he is conscious of his own love for himself; of his ardent concern for his earthly life; of the care with which he nourishes his body with food, clothing and all good things; of how he flees from death and avoids evil.
This is self-love, something we are aware of in ourselves.
What, then, does the commandment teach?
To do to another as you do to yourself; to value his body and his life as highly as your own body and life.
Now, how could God have pointed you to an example dearer, more pleasing and more to the purpose than this one—the deep instinct of your nature?
Indeed, the depth of your character is measured by the writing of this command in your heart.
36. How will it go with you before God if you do not love your neighbor?
Since you feel this commandment written within your heart, your conscience will condemn you.

Your whole conduct will be an example that witnesses against you, testifying that you failed to do to others as the natural instinct of your being—more forcefully than all the examples of the saints—has taught you to do.
But how will it go with the clergy in particular—the churchmen with their singing and praying, their cowls and shaven crowns, and all their trickery?
I say nothing about the fact that they have never kept the commandment.

I ask, however: when has their monastic fanaticism allowed them time and opportunity to perceive this law in their hearts even once, to become aware of the example set for them in their own human instinct, or even to read the precept in books or hear it preached?

Poor, miserable people! Do you presume to think that God will make void this commandment of love, so deeply and clearly impressed upon the heart, so beautifully and unmistakably illustrated in your own natures, and in the many written and spoken words as well—do you think God will do this on account of your cowls and shaven crowns, and have regard for what you have been devising and performing?
37. Alas, how shamelessly the world has ignored this beautiful and impressive commandment, in which the individual, the task, the model and the sphere of labor are so skillfully presented!
And, on the other hand, how shamefully it busies itself with the very reverse of what this commandment teaches!
Its whole practice and tendency seem to be to place our responsibility upon others; monks and priests must be righteous for us and pray in our place, so that we ourselves may be excused.
For the noblest virtue, love, we substitute self-devised works; in place of our neighbors we put wood and stone, clothing and food, even dead souls—the saints of heaven.
These we serve; with these we are occupied; they are the sphere in which we exercise ourselves.
Instead of the noblest example—“as yourself”—we look to the legends and the works of saints.

We presume to imitate such outward examples, neglecting the duty which our own nature and life present and which the command of God outlines, even though that duty offers more than we could ever fulfill.
Even if we could accomplish everything it offers, we would still not be equal to Christ.

blocks.x: Love Works Only Good to Its Neighbor.

s: “Love works no ill to its neighbor; love, therefore, is the fulfillment of the law.”
38. The Ten Commandments forbid doing evil to our neighbor—“You shall not kill, You shall not commit adultery,” and so on.
The apostle, using similar wording, says that love keeps all these commands, injuring no one.
Not only that; it brings about good for all.
It is practically doing evil to allow our neighbor to remain in danger when we can relieve him, even though we may have had no part in putting him where he is.
If he is hungry and we do not feed him when it is in our power to do so, we practically let him die of hunger.
We should take this view of any perilous condition, any adverse circumstance, in which our neighbors find themselves.
We have now heard how love is the fulfillment of the Law.
Text: Colossians 3:12-17.

12 Put on therefore, as God's elect, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, meekness, longsuffering; 13 bearing with one another and forgiving each other, if anyone has a complaint against anyone; just as the Lord forgave you, so must you also do. 14 And above all these things put on love, which is the bond of perfectness.
15 And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, for to this you were also called in one body; and be thankful.
16 Let the Word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to God.
17 And whatever you do, in word or in deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
1. This text is also a letter of admonition, teaching what kind of fruit properly results from faith.
Paul deals kindly with the Colossians.
He does not command, urge or threaten, as teachers of the Law must do with those who are under the Law.
He persuades them with loving words in view of the blessing and grace of God they have received, and in the light of Christ's own example.
Christians should act with readiness and cheerfulness, moved neither by fear of punishment nor by desire for reward, as has often been stated before.
This admonition has been repeated so often in the preceding epistle lesson that we know, I trust, what makes a Christian.
Therefore we will only touch briefly on the subject.
“Put on, therefore.”

2. In the epistle for New Year's Day we have sufficiently explained the meaning of “putting on”: how by faith we put on Christ, and he puts on us; how in love we put on our neighbor, and our neighbor puts on us.
The Christian's clothing is of two kinds—faith and love.
Christ wore two kinds of garments—one whole and representing faith, the other divided and representing love.
Paul here refers to the latter garment, love.
He would teach us Christians what kind of ornaments and apparel we are to wear in the world—not silk or precious gold.
These are forbidden to women by Peter (1 Peter 3:3) and by Paul (1 Timothy 2:9).
Love for our neighbor is a garment that suits us well—that love which leads us to concern ourselves with our neighbor and his misfortunes.
Such love is called the ornament of Christian character—an ornament in the eyes of men.
3. Notice the tender and sacred manner of the apostle's admonition, a manner he is accustomed to use toward us.
He does not drive us with laws, but persuades us by reminding us of the inexpressible grace of God; for he calls us the “elect of God,” and “holy” and “beloved.”
He would call forth the fruits of faith, desiring that they be yielded in a willing, cheerful and happy spirit.

The person who sincerely believes and trusts that before God he is beloved, holy and elect will consider how to maintain his honors and titles and how to conduct himself worthily of them; more than that, he will love God with such fervor that he can do or leave undone, or suffer, all things cheerfully, and he will never know how to do enough.
But he who doubts that God is so disposed toward him will not recognize the force of these words.
He will not feel the power of the statement that we are holy, beloved and elect in the sight of God.

4. Let us disregard, therefore, the saints who elect and love themselves; who adorn themselves with the works of the Law; who observe fasts and disciplines; who pay regard to clothing and position—for they are unwilling to be sinners before God.
Our ornaments are unlike these and have nothing to do with such mockeries.
They are honesty, sincerity, good works and service to our neighbor.
We are not bound by laws regarding food, clothing, times and the like.
We are holy in the sight of God, before whom no one can be holy until he sees himself as a sinner and rejects his own righteousness.
But the people just mentioned are holy in their own estimation; therefore they always remain wicked—sinners in the sight of God.
We are beloved of God because we despise ourselves; we judge and condemn ourselves and reject our self-love.
The others, because they love and esteem themselves, are despicable and unacceptable in the sight of God.
Again, we are chosen by God for the reason that we despise ourselves as filth.
Such people God chooses, and has chosen from eternity.
Because the would-be saints elect themselves, God will reject them, as indeed he has from eternity.
Now, this is what Paul means by these words:
“A heart of compassion.”

5. These words stand for part of the ornament, the beautiful, charming Christian jewel, which suits us better in the sight of God than pearls, precious stones, silk and gold suit us in the eyes of the world.
“A heart of compassion” is evidence of the true Christian.
Paul would say: “You are to be merciful not simply in outward deed or in appearance, but in the inmost heart.”
He refers to that sincere and wholehearted mercy found in the father and mother who see the distress of a child for whom they would readily risk their lives or give up all they possess.
The Christian's mind and heart should be constantly devoted to merciful deeds, with an ardor so intense that he is unaware he is doing good and compassionate acts.
6. With this single phrase Paul condemns the works and arbitrary rules of hypocritical saints, whose severity will not allow them to associate with sinners.
Their rigorous laws must control everything.
They do nothing but compel and drive.
They show no mercy, but only constant reproach, censure, condemnation, blame and bluster.
They can endure no imperfection.
But among Christians many are sinners, many are weak.
In fact, Christians associate only with these, not with saints.
Christians reject no one, but bear with all.
Indeed, they are as sincerely concerned for sinners as they would be for themselves if they were the weak ones.
They pray for sinners, teach, admonish, persuade, and do all in their power to win them back.
Such is the true character of a Christian.
So God, in Christ, has dealt with us and always deals with us.
So Christ dealt with the adulteress (John 8:11) when he set her free from her tormentors, and with his gracious words moved her to repentance and let her go.
We read that St. Antony said Paphrutius knew how souls are to be saved, because he rescued a certain man from brothers who persecuted and oppressed him for his transgression.
See the “Lives of the Fathers.”
If God were to deal with us according to the strictness of his laws, we would all be lost.
But he mercifully suspends the Law.
Isaiah says (9:4): “For the yoke of his burden, and the staff of his shoulder, the rod of his oppressor, you have broken.”
God now only persuades.
7. Note how entangled in the Law and in hypocrisy they still are who consider themselves eminent saints and at the same time are intolerant of the weaknesses of Christians.

If they fail to find perfect holiness—a miracle of purity—in those who possess Christ and know the Gospel, then nothing is as it should be; the heavens are about to fall and the earth about to be destroyed.
They can only judge, censure and mock, saying: “Oh, yes, he is truly evangelical; indeed, he is a visionary!”
In this way they reveal their utter blindness.
With the beam constantly in their own eyes, they show how little they know of Christ.

Know, then, when you meet someone so ready to censure and condemn, someone who demands absolute perfection in Christians—know that such a person is merely an enforcer of the Law, a base hypocrite, a merciless jailer, with no true knowledge of Christ.
Just as among Christians there is no law but all is love, so neither can there be judgment, condemnation and censure.
And he who calls another a visionary is certainly ten times a visionary himself.
In the very thing for which he judges and condemns another, he condemns himself.
Since he ignores mercy and everything but the Law, he finds no mercy in the sight of God; in fact, he has never experienced, never tasted, God's mercy.
To his taste, both God and neighbor are as bitter as gall and wormwood.
8. But tender mercy is to be shown only to Christians and only among Christians.
With those who reject and persecute the Gospel we must deal differently.
It is not right that my charity should be so liberal as to tolerate unsound doctrine.
In the case of false faith and doctrine there is neither love nor patience.
Against these it is my duty to contend earnestly and not to yield a hair's breadth.
Otherwise—when faith is not endangered—I must be unfailingly kind and merciful to all, notwithstanding the weaknesses of their lives.
I may not censure, oppress or drive; I must persuade, entreat and tolerate.
A defective life does not destroy Christianity; it exercises it.
But defective doctrine—false belief—destroys all good.
So, then, toleration and mercy are not permissible in the case of unsound doctrine; only anger, opposition and death are in order, yet always in accordance with the Word of God.
9. On the other hand, those who are mercifully tolerated must not imagine that, because they escape censure and force, their beliefs and practices are right.
They must not take such mercy as encouragement to become lazy and negligent and to continue in their error.
Mercy is not extended to them with any such intention.
The purpose is to give them opportunity to recover zeal and strength.
But if they are inclined to remain as they are, very well; let them alone.
