They will not continue so for long; the devil will lead them farther astray, until finally they fall away completely and even become enemies of the Gospel.
Such will be their end if they allow mercy to be lavished on them in vain.
We may not be lazy and asleep in the matter of our false doctrines, relying on the fact that we are not despised or constrained by men.
There is particular need to be active and diligent, for the devil neither sleeps nor rests.
We need to beware that he does not lead us where we will never enjoy God's mercy.
“Kindness, lowliness, meekness, longsuffering.”
10. These words represent the other elements of Christian character.
You will find kindness defined in the second epistle lesson for the early Christmas service.
It marks the conduct of the person who is gentle and sympathetic toward all, who repels no one with a forbidding face, harsh words or rude behavior.
We Germans would call such a person affable and friendly.
Kindness is a virtue not confined to certain works; it shapes the whole life.
The kind person is obliging to everyone, displeased with no one, and attractive to all people.
In contrast are those odd characters who take pleasure in nothing but their own notions; who insist that others adapt themselves to them and their ways, while they yield to no one.
Such people are called “uncivil.”
11. But the generosity of kindness is not to be extended to false doctrine.
It is to be exercised only in regard to conduct and works.
As has often been stated before, love with all its works and fruits has no place in the matter of unsound doctrine.
I must love my neighbor and show him kindness whatever the imperfections of his life.
But if he refuses to believe or to teach sound doctrine, I cannot, I dare not, love him or show him kindness.
According to Paul (Galatians 1:8-9), I must hold him excommunicated and accursed, even if he were an angel from heaven.
So remarkably do faith and love differ and stand apart.
Love will be, must be, kind even to the bitterest enemy so long as he does not assail faith and doctrine.
But it will not, it cannot, tolerate the person who does, be it father, mother or dearest friend.
Deuteronomy 13:6-8. Love, then, must be exercised not in relation to the doctrine and faith of our neighbor, but in relation to his life and works.
Faith, on the contrary, has to do not with his works and life, but with his doctrine and belief.
12. I think by this time we must know the meaning of “lowliness” of mind—esteeming oneself least and others greater.
Christ illustrates it by taking the lowest seat at the wedding, and doing so cheerfully.
We are to serve even when our service is not wanted, and to minister to our enemies.
So Christ humbled himself before Judas the betrayer, and before all of us.
He came not to be served, but to serve.
It is no wonder that humbleness of mind is a rare virtue, for every Christian grace is a rarity.
Graces are especially lacking among those who, professing to know most of Christ, find something to censure in all Christians.
Paul calls Christianity a mystery of God; and it is likely to remain one.
13. “Meekness” is the opposite of anger.
The meek person is not easily stirred to show anger, to curse, strike, hate or wish evil to anyone, even an enemy.
To refrain in this way is an art. Hypocrites—in fact, the whole world—can be meek toward friends and those who treat them well.
But true meekness and humility will remain only among the elect and beloved saints of God, as Paul implies here.
Even among these, many are lacking in all, or at least a large part, of the Christian graces.
So hypocrites may find something to censure, something to be offended at, in the beloved, elect saints of God.
And the true saints have occasion to exercise mercy, humility, meekness and forbearance.
Those whom Paul here calls elect and beloved saints of God, though somewhat lacking in humility, meekness and forbearance, are not therefore unholy, not rejected and despised.
14. Paul makes a distinction between longsuffering and forbearance, as in Romans 2:4: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering?”
In “longsuffering” we have the thought expressed here and there by God in the Psalms and elsewhere by the Hebrew “arich apaim”—“slow to wrath.”
God patiently bears with evil.
Indeed, he repeatedly delays vengeance, apparently more ready to forgive than to punish, even under extreme provocation and when he has just reason to chastise.
Longsuffering reaches farther than patience.
Patience bears evil and injustice; but longsuffering delays punishment.
It does not intend to punish; it would not take hasty revenge.
Unlike the vengeful, it wishes no one evil.
We see many, indeed, who suffer much and are patient, but at the same time trust in a final revenge.
The longsuffering Christian, however, is opposed to revenge and desires the sinner to amend his ways.
“Bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if anyone has a complaint against anyone; just as the Lord forgave you, so must you also do.”
15. In this verse all law is abolished among Christians.
No one is permitted to demand the recovery of his property through legal process.
He must forgive and yield.
Christ's example enjoins this principle; he has forgiven us.
And how far does his forgiveness extend?
He pardons past sins, but that is not all; as John says (1 John 2:1-2), “If anyone sins, we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins.”
16. Note that it is the true Christian saints whom Paul describes, yet he regards them as weak to the point of offending and complaining against one another.
This is a state of affairs by no means fitting for Christians and saints.
So I say Christ's kingdom is a mystery too obscure for our preaching and teaching to explain sufficiently.
Unbelievers cannot be induced to work, but believers cannot be kept from working.
Some would not believe and some would not love.
It is true of Christ's kingdom that his Christians are not perfectly holy.
They have begun to be holy and are in a state of progress.
Among them are still found anger, evil desire, unholy love, worldly care and other deplorable weaknesses, remnants of the old Adam.
Paul speaks of these things as burdens which one must bear for a neighbor (Galatians 6:2), and in Romans 15:1 he admonishes us to “bear the infirmities of the weak.”
Likewise Christ loved his apostles much and suffered much from them, and he still bears with his own daily.

17. Some, listing the fruits of the Spirit mentioned in Galatians 5:22-23, say a Christian should be gentle, meek, longsuffering and chaste; and they regard this passage as a law commanding such fruits.
Hence they refuse to recognize as Christians any who fail to possess these fruits in perfection.
Now, such people cannot believe there is a Christ, certain as the fact is.
They judge maliciously, complaining that Christians do not exist.
They take offense at Christ for his superior wisdom.
For Christ has given us scriptural authority for knowing Christians by their fruits.
He says (Matthew 7:16), “By their fruits you shall know them.”
Here they are emphatic.
18. Can you locate where such a person fails?
He fails in this: he understands absolutely nothing of Christ's kingdom.
For he misinterprets the passages referring to Christians.

He takes the statement that Christians should be kind and meek to mean that they must never become angry, must bear anything and show impatience toward no one; if they do not do so, they cannot be Christians, for they do not have the fruits.
Dear man, what but his own blindness can lead him to such a conclusion?
He imagines Christianity to be a holy order of perfection, altogether without weakness, a perfection like that in heaven among the angels.
But tell me, where do the Scriptures speak of Christians in this way?

But whoever recognizes Christianity as a progressive order still in its beginning will not be offended at the occasional display of ungentleness, unkindness and impatience on the part of a Christian; for he remembers that Christians are commanded to bear one another's burdens and weaknesses.
He knows that the list of the fruits of the Spirit is not a record of laws that must be observed or else Christ will be denied.
He is aware that the passage is to be interpreted as meaning that Christians are to strive to be kind; that is the mark at which they aim.
However, even though they have made a beginning and some progress in this virtue, they are often unkind and bear fruits directly opposite to the fruits of the Spirit.
True, the text quoted says we should be kind, but it does not say we are kind.
We are tending toward it; we are in a state of progress; but during the progress much of the old and not yet transformed nature is mixed in.

19. Know, then, that in a mysterious way Christ is in his saints, and beware of judging or condemning anyone when you do not have positive assurance that he believes and teaches contrary to the Gospel.
But whoever does oppose the Gospel you may safely judge to be without Christ and under the sway of the devil.
Pray for such a person and admonish him, in the hope of his conversion.
But in the case of one who embraces and honors the Gospel, observe Paul's comment (Romans 14:4): “Who are you who judge the servant of another? To his own lord he stands or falls.
Yes, he shall be made to stand; for the Lord has power to make him stand.”
And again (1 Corinthians 10:12): “Therefore let the one who thinks he stands take heed that he does not fall.”
Christ would be at the same time hidden and revealed, found and not found.
He permits some weaknesses to be mixed with the fruits of the Spirit, so that he may conceal himself and so that malicious judges may be offended.
“And above all these things put on love, which is the bond of perfectness.”
20. From longsuffering and meekness the apostle distinguishes love and the other jewels of spiritual beauty of which we have already heard, though all are included in love.
As faith is the chief element of Christian character, so love is the chief of the fruits of the Spirit, the jewel of surpassing beauty.
Therefore Paul says, “Above all these things put on love.”
Love surpasses mercy, kindness, meekness and humility.
Paul calls it “the bond of perfectness” because it unites human hearts—not a partial unity, based on likeness or close kinship, but a complete unity among all people and in all relations.
It makes us of one mind, one heart, one desire.
It permits no one to start a peculiar order of doctrine or faith.
All who love hold the same belief.
Consequently there is the same purpose of heart with the poor and the rich, with rulers and subjects, the sick and the well, the high and the low, the honored and the disgraced.
The loving heart lets all share in its good; more than that, it shares in the adversities of all people, regarding them as its own.
Where love is, perfect unity and fellowship prevail in every event, good or bad.
It is a most perfect bond.
21. Where love is lacking, hearts are united and aims are one in only a few matters; in most things there is disagreement.
For instance: robbers have a common bond, but it is no more than a common purpose in committing robbery and murder.
Worldly friends are of one mind as far as their own interests are concerned.
Monks are united with regard to their order and their honor.
Herod and Pilate agreed, but only with regard to Christ.
For the most part it is rare that one monk, priest or layman agrees with another.
Their bond of union is weak; they are like chaff bound with straw.
“And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, for to this you were also called.”
22. There is much that threatens to break love's bond.
The devil never sleeps, but continually stirs up discord and unrest.
Paul does not deny that the bond is attacked.
But he urges us to resist, remembering that love must be exercised through opposition.
He admonishes us to let the peace of Christ have dominion in our hearts.

The thought of the verse is this: Though the peace of the world and the flesh does not last, though you must witness the forces of discord and disruption, nevertheless let your hearts have peace in Christ.
We spoke of the peace of God in the epistle selection for the Fourth Sunday in Advent—Philippians 4:7.
This is the peace to which the Gospel calls—not the peace of the world, the flesh or the devil, but the peace that surpasses all understanding, of which Paul tells us.
We are to hold on to the peace of God not only when all is well, but when sin, death, the flesh, the world and all calamities rage.
“And be thankful.”

23. “Thankfulness” here may be taken in either of two senses. First, thankfulness toward God, Paul's thought being: Let the remembrance of all God has done for you move you to gratitude for his grace and mercy, a gratitude which love and peace shall follow.
Secondly, we may understand thankfulness toward men—gratitude for all the benefits received from our fellow men.
The apostle elsewhere (2 Timothy 3:2) speaks of there being in the last days, among other vices, that of “unthankfulness” of people toward one another.
Let everyone choose for himself between the two applications.

It is my opinion—since Paul later takes up the subject of gratitude to God, and since he is here dealing with love to our neighbor—it is my opinion that he refers here to gratitude toward our fellow men.
This, I think, is his meaning.
Man is glad to have love shown to him; he is quite willing to receive good from others and to be dealt with according to the Gospel.
At the same time, he is not inclined to show love to his fellows: favors shown him are lost on his ingratitude.

Though love is not defeated by ungratefulness—for it bears all things (1 Corinthians 13:7)—yet unthankfulness produces weariness and aversion; and it is a base, unjust and shameful thing for one who continually gives help not to be served in return.
24. Paul says on this topic (Galatians 6:6), “Let the one who is taught in the Word share with the one who teaches in all good things.”
And he declares (1 Timothy 5:17) that those who labor in the Word and doctrine are worthy of double honor.

In the ninth chapter of First Corinthians he speaks at length of how teachers are entitled to support, saying that the mouth of the threshing ox should not be muzzled; that would be gross ingratitude.
He hints here at such unthankfulness.
It is true today, and always has been, that preachers of the Word of God must generally seek their own bread, and receive ingratitude as their reward for the wonderful blessings they bring.
If it were their part to celebrate masses and indulgences, gratitude would be forthcoming; great would be the gifts and service rendered them as an expression of thankfulness.
But the Levites under the old Law were treated just as ungratefully, in contrast with the favor shown to the priests of idols and groves.
“Let the Word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to God.”
25. This verse fittingly follows the command to be thankful.
Paul would say: Be careful to honor teachers and preachers, being grateful that they handle the Word and may richly impart it to you.
I do not imagine Paul refers to the giving of the Word of God from heaven, for it is not in man's power to give it so; God alone can entrust it to us.
So he has done and continues to do.
Whenever he permits the Gospel to be preached, he showers the message on us abundantly, withholding no essential knowledge.
But after it is given, we ought to be thankful and faithfully read and hear it, sing and speak it, and meditate on it day and night.
And it should be our part to secure enough teachers to minister it to us generously and continuously.
This is what is meant by letting the Word of God dwell among us richly.
26. Satisfied, lazy spirits soon grow tired and dismiss their pastors to go wherever they like.
The pastors are forced to seek a living by other work, and so God's Word is neglected and becomes rare and thinly sown in the land.
Nehemiah (13:10) complains that the Levites, for lack of support, were forced to leave their worship and temple and flee to the fields, or to start false worship and fables to mislead the people.
Then they received enough to live on—they became wealthy.

It has come about in the Christian Church that as often as the support of godly pastors and teachers has become a burden, as Augustine laments has been the case, they have been either forced to neglect the Word in order to labor for their own support, or forced to invent that wretched, accursed worship now prevalent throughout the world, by which the preachers have attained lordly position.
With the revival of the Gospel the financial difficulty mentioned is recurring, and it will continue to recur.

One hundred dollars cannot now be raised for the support of a good schoolmaster or preacher where formerly a thousand dollars—yes, incalculable sums—were contributed toward churches, institutions, masses, vigils and the like.

Once more God punishes ingratitude by allowing his preachers to withdraw entirely from the ministry and to provide for their own support, or by sending on the people even greater delusions than ever, which rob them of their wealth and destroy body and soul.
For they refuse to let the Word of God dwell among them richly.
Paul adds the qualifying phrase:
“In all wisdom.”

27. If we were to have the Word of God so richly that it rang out on every street corner and was sung everywhere by all children—as those intended who brought canonical prayers and singing and reading into the pulpits and the lessons—what would all this profit without an understanding mind, without wisdom?
For the Word of God was given to make us wise.
It was intended that we should understand it, and that it should be preached and sung intelligibly.
And those who minister it, who sing and speak it, ought to be wise, understanding everything that pertains to the salvation of the soul and the honor of God.
That is what it means to have the Word of God dwell among us in all wisdom.
Here Paul briefly overthrows the noisy practices of the churches and monasteries, where so much preaching and reading goes on while at the same time the Gospel is not understood.

He seems to have foreseen the coming time when the Word of God would freely prevail, but with no resulting wisdom; the time when men would daily increase in ignorance and fanaticism until they became mere dolts, so completely void of wisdom as to call shouting and boasting divine worship, and to regard that as preaching the salvation of souls.
28. What it is to teach and to admonish has often been explained.
Here Paul makes the duty of instruction common to all Christians—“teaching and admonishing one another.”
That is, apart from the regular office of preaching, each is to teach himself and others, thus making everyday use of the Word of God, publicly and privately, generally and specifically.

29. As I see it, the apostle's distinction among the three words—psalms, hymns and spiritual songs—is this: “psalms” properly means those compositions of David and others that make up the Book of Psalms; “hymns” refers to the songs of the prophets mentioned here and there in the Scriptures—songs of Moses, Deborah, Solomon, Isaiah, Daniel, Habakkuk, with the Magnificat, the Benediction, and the like, called “Canticles”; “spiritual songs” are those not written in the Scriptures but daily composed by men.
Paul calls these latter “spiritual” to a greater degree than psalms and hymns, though he recognizes those too as spiritual.
He forbids worldly, sensual and unbecoming songs, desiring us to sing of spiritual things.
It is then that our songs are fitted to benefit and instruct, as he says.
30. But what is the meaning of Paul's phrase “with grace”?

I offer the explanation that he refers to the grace of God and means that the singing of spiritual songs is to be voluntary, uncompelled, spontaneous, rendered with cheerfulness and prompted by love—not extorted by authority and law, as the singing in our churches is today.
No one sings, preaches or prays from a recognition of mercy and grace received.

The motive is a hope of gain, or a fear of punishment, injury and shame; or again, the holiest people bind themselves to obedience, or are driven to it, for the sake of winning heaven, and not at all to further the knowledge of the Word of God—the understanding of it richly and in all wisdom, as Paul desires it to be understood.
I imagine Paul has in mind the charm of music and the beauty of poetry that belong to song.
He says in Ephesians 4:29: “Let no corrupt speech come out of your mouth, but such as is good for building up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.”
Likewise songs should be fitted to bring grace and favor to those who hear.
Foul, unchaste and superfluous words have no place in them, nor any unfitting elements—elements void of meaning and without virtue and life.
Hymns are to be rich in meaning, pleasing and sweet, and so a source of enjoyment for all hearers.
The singing of such songs is very properly called in Hebrew singing “with grace,” as Paul has it.
Of this kind are the psalms and hymns of the Scriptures; they are good thoughts presented in pleasing words.

Some songs, though expressed in charming words, are worldly and carnal; while others that present good thoughts are at the same time expressed in words that are unfitting, unattractive and devoid of grace.
“Singing with grace in your hearts to God.”
31. Paul does not command silence of the lips.

He would have the words of the mouth come from the heart sincerely and fervently—not hypocritically, as Isaiah mentions (29:13), saying: “This people draw near to me, and with their mouth and with their lips they honor me, but they have removed their heart far from me.”

Paul would have the Word of God dwell among Christians generally, and be richly spoken, sung and meditated upon everywhere—and that with understanding and producing spiritual fruit, the Word being prized by all.
He would have men thus sing heartfelt praise and thanks to the Lord.
He says let the Word “dwell” among you.
Not merely lodge as a guest for a night or two, but abide with you forever.
He is constantly wary of human doctrines.
“And whatever you do, in word or in deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.”
32. The works of Christians are not limited by name, time or place.
Whatever Christians do is good; whenever it is done, it is timely; wherever it is wrought, it is fitting.
So Paul names no work.
He makes no distinction, but concludes that all works are good, whether it be eating or drinking, speaking or keeping silent, waking or sleeping, going or staying, being idle or otherwise.
All acts are supremely worthy because they are done in the name of the Lord Jesus.
Such is Paul's teaching here.
And our works are done in the name of the Lord Jesus when by faith we hold fast to the fact that Christ is in us and we in him, in the sense that we no longer labor, but he lives and works in us.
Paul says (Galatians 2:20), “It is no longer I that live, but it is Christ who lives in me.”
But when we do a work as of ourselves, then it is done in our own name and there is nothing good about it.
33. The expression “in the name of God,” or “Go in the name of Jesus,” is often spoken falsely and in sheer hypocrisy.
The saying goes, “All misfortunes rise in the name of God.”
For teachers of false doctrines habitually offer their wares in the name of God.
They even come in the name of Christ, as he himself foretells.
Matthew 24:24. To speak and work sincerely and earnestly in Jesus' name, the heart must necessarily agree with what the mouth says.
As the lips speak in the name of God, so the heart must confidently, with firm faith, hold that God directs and performs the work.
Peter teaches the same (1 Peter 4:11): “If anyone ministers [performs anything], ministering as from the strength that God supplies.”
Then the venture will prosper.
No Christian should undertake any deed in his own ability and directed by his own judgment.
Rather, let him be assured that God works with and through him.
Paul says (1 Corinthians 9:26): “I therefore run in this way, not uncertainly; I fight in this way, not as beating the air.”
34. Such an attitude will result in praise and thanks to God as the one to whom all honor and praise are due for every good thing.
So Paul teaches, and Peter also.
Immediately after declaring that we are to work according to the ability God gives, Peter adds “so that God may be glorified in all things through Jesus Christ.”
But he who undertakes anything in his own ability, however much he may glorify God with his lips, lies and deceives, like the hypocrite in the Gospel.
Thankfulness, therefore, is the only duty we can perform toward God; and this is not to be rendered of ourselves, but through our Mediator, Jesus.
Without him no one can come to the Father, no one can be accepted.
We have often spoken of this fact.
Text: First Corinthians 13.
1 If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal.
2 And if I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing.
3 And if I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing.

4 Love suffers long and is kind; love does not envy; love does not vaunt itself, is not puffed up, 5 does not behave improperly, does not seek its own, is not provoked, keeps no account of evil; 6 does not rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth; 7 bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.
8 Love never fails; but whether there are prophecies, they will be done away; whether there are tongues, they will cease; whether there is knowledge, it will be done away.
9 For we know in part, and we prophesy in part; 10 but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be done away.
11 When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I felt as a child, I thought as a child; now that I have become a man, I have put away childish things.
12 For now we see in a mirror, darkly; but then face to face. Now I know in part; but then I shall know fully, even as I also was fully known.
13 But now faith, hope, love abide, these three; and the greatest of these is love.
1. Paul's purpose in this chapter is to silence and humble haughty Christians, particularly teachers and preachers.
The Gospel gives much knowledge of God and of Christ, and conveys many wonderful gifts, as Paul recounts in Romans 12 and in First Corinthians 12.
He tells us that some have the gift of speaking, some of teaching, some of explaining Scripture; others of ruling; and so on.
Among Christians are great riches of spiritual knowledge, great treasures in the way of spiritual gifts.
The meaning of God, Christ, conscience, the present and the future life, and similar things is plain to all.
But few indeed are to be found who make the right use of such gifts and knowledge, who humble themselves to serve others, as love directs.
Each seeks his own honor and advantage, desiring to gain promotion and precedence over others.
2. We see today how the Gospel has given men knowledge beyond anything known in the world before, and has bestowed on them new capabilities.
Various gifts have been showered upon them and distributed among them, which have brought them honor.
But they go on heedless.
No one considers how he may, in Christian love, serve his fellow men for their benefit.
Each seeks glory and honor, advantage and wealth for himself.

If one could secure for himself the distinction of being the only person learned and powerful in the Gospel, with all others insignificant and useless, he would gladly do it; he would be glad if he alone could be regarded as Mister Smart.
At the same time he puts on deep humility and great self-abasement, and preaches about love and faith.
But he would find it hard if, in practice, he had to touch with his little finger what he preaches.
This explains why the world is so filled with fanatics and schismatics, and why every man wants to master and outrank all others.
Such people are haughtier than those who taught them.

Paul here attacks these vainglorious spirits and judges them to be wholly insignificant, however great their knowledge may be and however much greater their gifts, unless they humble themselves and use their gifts in the service of others.

To these coarse and mean people he addresses himself with a multitude of words and a lengthy discourse, a subject he elsewhere disposes of in a few words; for instance, where he says (Philippians 2:3-4), "In lowliness of mind each counting the other better than himself; each of you not looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others."
By way of illustration, he would pass sentence on himself should he be guilty in this way, in order to warn all the more forcefully others who fall far short of his standing. He says,
"If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels."

4. That is, though I had the ability to teach and to preach with power beyond that of any man or angel, with words of perfect charm, with truth and excellence informing my message—though I could do this, "but do not have love [charity]," and only seek my own honor and profit and not my neighbor's, "I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal."
In other words, "I might perhaps teach others something by it, might fill their ears with sound, but before God I would be nothing."

As a clock or a bell has no power to hear its own sound and gains no benefit from its own stroke, so the preacher who lacks love cannot himself understand anything he says, nor does he thereby improve his standing before God.
He has much knowledge, indeed, but because he fails to place it in the service of love, it is the quality of his knowledge that is at fault.
1 Corinthians 8:1-12.
Far better that he were mute or lacking in eloquence, if only he teaches in love and meekness, than that he should speak like an angel while seeking only his own interests.
"And if I have the gift of prophecy."
5. According to chapter 14, to prophesy is to be able, by the Holy Spirit's inspiration, to understand and explain the prophets and the Scriptures correctly.
This is a most excellent gift.

To "know mysteries" is to be able to grasp the spiritual meaning of the Scriptures, or their allegorical references, as Paul does where (Galatians 4:24-31) he makes Sarah and Hagar represent the two covenants, and Isaac and Ishmael the two peoples—the Jews and the Christians.

Christ does the same (John 3:14) when he makes the bronze serpent of Moses a type of himself on the cross; again, when Isaac, David, Solomon and other figures of sacred history appear as figures of Christ.
Paul calls it "mystery"—this hidden, secret meaning beneath the primary sense of the narrative.
But "knowledge" is the understanding of practical matters, such as Christian liberty, or the realization that the conscience is not bound.

Paul would say, then: "Though one may understand the Scriptures, both in their obvious and in their hidden sense; though he may know all about Christian liberty and proper conduct; yet if he does not have love, if he does not serve his neighbor with that knowledge, it is all of no use whatever; in God's sight he is nothing."
6. Note how forcefully yet kindly Paul restrains the disgraceful vice of vainglory.
He disregards even those exalted gifts, those gifts of exceeding refinement, charm and excellence, which naturally produce pride and haughtiness while they command the admiration and esteem of men.
Who would not suppose the Holy Spirit to dwell visibly where such wisdom, such discernment of the Scriptures, is present?
Paul's two epistles to the Corinthians are almost wholly directed against this particular vice, for it creates much mischief wherever it holds sway.
In Titus 1:7 he names first among the virtues of a bishop that he be "non superbus," not haughty.
In other words, that he not exalt himself because of his office, his honor and his understanding, and despise others by comparison.
But strangely Paul says,
"If I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing."

blocks.x: Love, the Fruit of the Spirit Received by Faith.

s: 7. We hold, and it is unquestionably true, that it is faith which justifies and cleanses.
But if it justifies and purifies, love must be present.
The Spirit cannot but impart love together with faith.
In fact, where true faith is, the Holy Spirit dwells; and where the Holy Spirit is, there must be love and every excellence.
How is it, then, that Paul speaks as if faith without love were possible?
We reply: this one text cannot be understood as overturning and contradicting all those texts which ascribe justification to faith alone.
Even the sophists have not attributed justification to love, nor is this possible, for love is an effect, or fruit, of the Spirit, who is received through faith.
8. Three answers may be given to the question.
First, Paul is not referring here to the Christian faith, which is inevitably accompanied by love, but to a general faith in God and his power.
Such faith is a gift, as are, for instance, the gift of tongues, the gift of knowledge, of prophecy, and the like.
There is reason to believe that Judas performed miracles in spite of the absence of Christian faith, according to John 6:70: "One of you is a devil."
This general faith, powerless to justify or to cleanse, allows the old man with his vices to remain, just as do the gifts of intellect, health, eloquence and riches.

9. A second answer is: Though Paul refers to the true Christian faith, he has in mind those who have indeed attained to faith and performed miracles with it, but fall from grace through pride, and so lose their faith.
Many begin but do not continue.
They are like the seed on stony ground.
They soon fall from faith.
The temptations of vainglory are mightier than those of adversity.
One who has the true faith and is at the same time able to perform miracles is likely to seek and accept honor so eagerly as to fall from both love and faith.
10. A third answer is: Paul, in his effort to present the necessity of love, supposes an impossible condition.
For instance, I might express myself this way: "Though you were a god, if you lacked patience you would be nothing."
That is, patience is so essential to divinity that divinity itself could not exist without it—a proposition necessarily true.

So Paul's meaning is not that faith could exist without love, but on the contrary, that love is so much an essential of faith that even mountain-moving faith would be nothing without love, if we could separate the two even in theory.
The third answer pleases me by far the best, though I do not reject the others, particularly the first.
For Paul's very first premise is impossible—"if I speak in the tongues of angels."
To speak with an angelic tongue is impossible for a human being, and he clearly emphasizes this impossibility by making a distinction between the tongues of men and those of angels.
There is no angelic tongue; while angels may speak to us in a human tongue, men can never speak in those of angels.

11. Just as we are to understand the first clause—"If I speak in the tongues of angels"—as meaning, Were it as possible as it is impossible for me to speak in the tongues of angels; so we are to understand the second clause—"If I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains"—to mean, Were it as possible as it is impossible to have such faith.
Equally impossible is the proposition of understanding all mysteries, and we must take it to mean, Were it possible for one to understand all mysteries, which, however, it is not.
John, in the last chapter of his Gospel, asserts that the world could not contain all the books that might be written concerning the things of the kingdom.
For no man can ever fathom the depths of these mysteries.

Paul's manner of expressing himself is simply a very common one, such as: "Even if I were a Christian, if I did not believe in Christ I would be nothing"; or, "Even if you were a prince, if you neither ruled men nor possessed property you would be nothing."
"And if I give away all my goods to feed the poor."
12. In other words, "Were I to perform all the good works on earth and yet did not have charity—having sought in them only my own honor and profit and not my neighbor's—I would nevertheless be lost."
In the performance of external works as great as the surrender of property and life, Paul includes all works that can possibly be performed, for he who would do these at all would do any work.
Just so, when he refers to tongues he includes all good words and doctrines; and in prophecy, understanding and faith he takes in all wisdom and knowledge.
Some may risk body and property for the sake of temporal glory.
So Romans and pagans have done; but since love was lacking and they sought only their own interests, they in effect gave nothing.

Since it is generally impossible for men to give away all their property and their bodies to be burned, the meaning must be: "Were it possible for me to give all my goods to the poor, and my body to be burned."
13. The false reasoning of the sophists will not stand when they maliciously deduce from this text the theory that the Christian faith is not effective to blot out sin and to justify.
They say that before faith can justify it must be adorned with love; but justification and its distinctive qualities as well are beyond their understanding.
Justification necessarily precedes love.
One does not love until he has become godly and righteous.
Love does not make us godly, but when one has become godly, love is the result.
Faith, the Spirit and justification have love as their effect and fruit, and not as a mere ornament and supplement.
We maintain that faith alone justifies and saves.
But so that we may not deceive ourselves and put our trust in a false faith, God requires love from us as the evidence of our faith, so that we may be sure that our faith is real faith.

blocks.x: The Nature of Christian Love.

s: "Love suffers long and is kind."
14. Now Paul begins to describe the nature of love, enabling us to perceive where real love and faith are to be found.
A haughty teacher does not possess the virtues the apostle lists.
Lacking these, however many gifts the haughty have received through the Gospel, they are devoid of love.
First, love "suffers long."
That is, it is patient; not sudden and swift to anger, not quick to give way to revenge, impatience or blind rage.
Rather it bears patiently with the wicked and the weak until they yield.
Haughty teachers can only judge, condemn and despise others, while justifying and exalting themselves.
15. Second, love is "kind."
In other words, it is pleasant to deal with; it is not forbidding in appearance; it ignores no one; it is kind to all men, in words, acts and attitude.
16. Third, love "does not envy"—it is not envious nor displeased at the greater prosperity of others; it grudges no one property or honor.
Haughty teachers, however, are envious and unkind.
They begrudge everyone else both honor and possessions.
Though with their lips they may pretend otherwise, these traits are plainly visible in their deeds.
17. Fourth, love "does not vaunt itself."
It is averse to trickery, to crafty guile and double-dealing.
Haughty and deceptive spirits cannot refrain from such conduct, but love deals honestly and uprightly and face to face.
18. Fifth, love is not "puffed up," as false teachers are, who swell themselves up like adders.

19. Sixth, love "does not behave improperly" after the manner of the passionate, impatient and obstinate—those who presume to be always in the right, who oppose all men and yield to none, and who insist on submission from every individual, or else they set the world on fire, bluster and fume, shriek and complain, and thirst for revenge.
That is what the inflating pride and haughtiness of which we have just spoken lead to.
20. Seventh, love "does not seek her own."
She does not seek financial advancement; not honor, profit, ease; not the preservation of body and life.
Rather she risks all these in her ... is no such thing as the Church of Christ nor as true Christians.
Many erring spirits, especially strong pretenders to ...
21. Eighth, love "is not [easily] provoked" by wrong and ingratitude; it is meek.
False teachers can tolerate nothing; they seek only their own advantage and honor, to the injury of others.
22. Ninth, love "keeps no account of [thinks no] evil."
It is not suspicious; it puts the best construction on everything and takes all in good faith.
The haughty, however, are immeasurably suspicious; always anxious not to be underrated, they put the worst construction on everything, as Joab construed Abner's deeds.
2 Samuel 3:25.
This is a shameful vice, and those who are guilty of it are hard to handle.
23. Tenth, love "does not rejoice in unrighteousness [iniquity]."
The words admit of two interpretations: first, as referring to the delight of an individual in his own evil doings.
Solomon (Proverbs 2:14) speaks of those who "rejoice to do evil."

Such people must be either extremely profligate and shameless, characters like harlots and scoundrels; or else they must be hypocrites, who do not recognize the wickedness of their conduct—characters like heretics and schismatics, who rejoice when their knavery succeeds under the name of God and of the truth.
I do not accept this interpretation, but the other.

Paul's meaning is that false teachers are malicious enough to prefer to hear, above all things, that someone else does wrong, commits error and is brought to shame; and their motive is simply that they themselves may appear upright and godly.
Such was the attitude of the Pharisee toward the tax collector, in the Gospel.
But love's compassion reaches far beyond its own sins, and prays for others.
24. Eleventh, love "rejoices with [in] the truth."
Here is evidence that the preceding phrase is to be taken as referring to malicious rejoicing at another's sin and fall.
Rejoicing in the truth is simply exulting in the right-doing and integrity of another.
Similarly, love is grieved at another's wrongdoing.
But to the haughty it is an affliction to learn of uprightness in someone else; for they imagine that such integrity detracts from their own profit and honor.
25. Twelfth, love "bears all things."
It excuses every failing in all men, however weak, unjust or foolish one may appear, and no one can be guilty of a wrong too great for it to overlook.
But no one can do right in the eyes of the haughty, who always find something to belittle and censure as beyond toleration, even if they must hunt up an old fence to find the injury.
26. Thirteenth, love "believes all things."
Paul does not refer here to faith in God, but to faith in men.
His meaning is: Love is of a decidedly trusting disposition.
The one who possesses it believes and trusts all men, considering them just and upright like himself.
He anticipates no sly and crooked dealing, but allows himself to be deceived, deluded, mocked and imposed upon, at every man's pleasure, and asks, "Do you really believe men are so wicked?"
He measures all other hearts by his own, and makes mistakes with the utmost cheerfulness.
But such error does him no injury.
He knows that God cannot forsake him, and that the one who deceives love only deceives himself.
The haughty, on the contrary, trust no one, will believe no one, and will not tolerate being deceived.
27. Fourteenth, love "hopes all things."
Love despairs of no man, however wicked he may be.
It hopes for the best.
As is implied here, love says, "We must indeed hope for better things."
It is plain from this that Paul is not referring to hope in God.
Love is a virtue particularly representing devotion to a neighbor; his welfare is its goal in thought and deed.
Like its faith, the hope that love holds is frequently misplaced, but it never gives up.
Love rejects no man; it despairs of no cause.
But the proud quickly despair of men in general, rejecting them as of no account.
28. Fifteenth, love "endures all things."
It endures whatever harm befalls it, whatever injury it suffers; it endures when its faith and hope in men have been misplaced; it endures when it sustains damage to body, property or honor.
It knows that no harm has been done, since it has a rich God.
False teachers, however, bear with nothing, least of all with treachery and the breaking of a pledged word.
29. Sixteenth, love never fails; that means it abides forever, also in the life to come.

It never gives up, never allows itself to be hindered or defeated by the wickedness or ingratitude of men, as do worldly individuals and false saints, who, as soon as they perceive contempt or ingratitude, draw back, unwilling to do further good to anyone, and, making themselves quite inhuman, become perfect misanthropes, like Timon in his reputation among the Greeks.
Love does not do so.
It does not allow itself to be made wicked by the wickedness of men, nor to be hindered in doing good.
It continues to do good everywhere, teaching and admonishing, helping and serving, even though its services and benefits must be repaid, not with good, but with evil.
Love remains constant and immovable; it continues, it endures, in this earthly life and also in the life to come.
The apostle adds, "Whether there are prophecies, they will be done away; whether there are tongues, they will cease; whether there is knowledge, it will be done away."
Love he commends above all other endowments, as a gift that can never pass away, even in the life to come.
Those other gifts, the boast of the false apostles, are given only for this present life, to serve in carrying out the ministerial office.
Prophecy, tongues, knowledge—all must cease; for in the life beyond each individual will himself perceive perfectly, and there will be no need for one to teach another.
Likewise, all differences, all inequalities, shall be no more.
No knowledge and no diversity of gifts is necessary; God himself will be all in every soul.
1 Corinthians 15:28.
30. Here Paul expresses the distinction between the life of faith here below and that heavenly life of divine vision.
He would teach that we have the same possession in this life and in the other, for it is the same God and the same treasures which we have here by faith and there by sight.
In the objects themselves there is no difference; the difference lies in our knowledge.
We have the same God in both lives, but in a different manner of possession.
The mode of possessing God in this life is faith.
Faith is an imperfect, obscure vision, which makes the Word necessary, and the Word, in turn, gains currency through the ministry, tongues and prophecy.
Without the Word, faith cannot live.
But the mode of possessing God in the future life is not faith but sight.
This is perfect knowledge, making the Word unnecessary, and likewise preaching, tongues and prophecy.
These, then, must pass away. Paul continues,
"We know in part, and we prophesy in part."
31. "We know in part"; that is, in this life we know imperfectly, for it is by faith and not by sight.
And we "prophesy in part"; that is, imperfectly, for the substance of our prophecy is the Word and preaching.
Both knowledge and prophecy, however, reveal nothing less than what the angels see—the one God.
"But when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be done away."
He proves this by way of illustration and contrasts the child with the man.
For children, who are still weak, play is a necessity; it is a substitute for office and work.
Similarly, we in the present life are far too frail to behold God.
Until we are able, it is necessary that we use the medium of Word and faith, which are suited to our limitations.
"For now we see in a mirror [through a glass] darkly; but then face to face."
32. Faith, Paul tells us, is like a mirror, like a riddle.
The actual face is not in the glass; there is only the image of it.
Likewise, faith gives us not the radiant countenance of the eternal Deity, but a mere image of him, an image derived through the Word.
As a dark riddle points to something more than it expresses, so faith suggests something clearer than what it perceives.
But in the life to come, mirror and riddle, faith and its demonstration, shall all have ceased to be.
God's face and our own shall be mutually and clearly revealed.
Paul says, "Now I know in part; but then I shall know fully, even as I also was fully known [know even as I also am known]."
That is, God now knows me perfectly, clearly and plainly; no dark veil is upon me.
But as to him, a dark veil hides him from me.
With the same perfect clearness with which he now knows me, I shall then know him—without a veil.
The veil shall be taken away, not from him, but from me; for upon him there is no veil.

blocks.x: The Greatest Christian Virtue Is Love.

s: "But now faith, hope, love abide, these three; and the greatest of these is love."
33. The sophists have gone astray in a masterly manner with regard to this verse.
They have made faith vastly inferior to love because of Paul's statement that love is greater than faith and greater than hope.
As usual, their mad reason blindly seizes upon the literal expression.
They hack a piece out of it and ignore the rest.
Thus they fail to understand Paul's meaning; they do not perceive that Paul's sense concerning the greatness of love is expressed both in the text and in the context.
For surely it cannot be disputed that the apostle is here referring to the permanent or temporary character, respectively, of love and the other gifts, and not to their rank or power.
As to rank, not only faith but also the Word surpasses love; for the Word is the power of God bringing salvation to all who believe.
Romans 1:16. Yet the Word must pass away.
But though love is the fruit of the Word and its effect, it shall never be abolished.
Faith possesses God himself.
It possesses and can accomplish all things; yet it must cease.
Love gives to and blesses the neighbor, as a result of faith, and it shall never be done away.
34. Now, Paul's statement that love is greater than faith and hope is intended as an expression of the permanence, or eternal duration, of love.
Faith, being limited in time in comparison with love, ranks beneath it by reason of this temporary duration.
With the same right I might say that the kingdom of Christ is greater upon earth than Christ was.

By this I do not mean that the Church in itself is better and of higher rank than Christ, but merely that it covers a greater part of the earth than he covered; for he was here only three years, and those he spent in a limited sphere, whereas his kingdom has existed from the beginning and extends as far as the earth.
In this sense love is longer and broader than either faith or hope.
Faith deals with God merely in the heart and in this life, whereas the relations of love both to God and to the whole world are eternal.

Nevertheless, just as Christ is immeasurably better and higher and more precious than the Christian Church, although we see him moving within narrower limits and as a single individual, so faith is better, higher and more precious than love, though its duration is limited and it has God alone for its object.
35. Paul's purpose in thus extolling love is to strike a blow at false teachers and to bring to nothing their boasts about faith and other gifts when love is lacking.
His thought is: "If you do not possess love, which abides forever, then, since everything else you boast of is perishable, you will perish with it.

While the Word of God and spiritual gifts are eternal, yet the external office and proclamation of the Word, and likewise the use of gifts in their variety, shall have an end, and so your glory and pride shall become as ashes."
So then, faith justifies through the Word and produces love.

But while both Word and faith shall pass away, righteousness and love, which they bring about, abide forever; just as a building erected with the aid of scaffolding remains after the scaffolding has been removed.
36. Observe how small the word "love" is, and how easily spoken!
Who would have thought to find so much precious virtue and power ascribed by Paul to this one excellence, as the counterpart of so much that is evil?
This is, I think, magnifying love, painting love.
It is a better discourse on virtue and vice than the heathen writings are.
The model the apostle presents should justly shame the false teachers, who talk much of love but in whom not one of the virtues he mentions is found.
Every quality of love he names means false teachers buffeted and assaulted.
Whenever he magnifies love and describes her powers, he always at the same time makes a thrust at those who are lacking in any of them.
Well may we, then, as he describes the several features, add the comment, "But you do quite differently."

37. It is exceedingly strange that teachers without love should possess such gifts as Paul has mentioned here, namely, speaking in tongues, prophesying, understanding mysteries; that they should have faith, should give away their goods and allow themselves to be burned.

For we have seen what abominations follow where love is lacking; such individuals are proud, envious, puffed up, impatient, unstable, false, venomous, suspicious, malicious, disdainful, bitter, unwilling to serve, distrustful, selfish, ambitious and haughty.
How can it consistently be claimed that people of this kind can, through faith, remove mountains, give their bodies to be burned, prophesy, and so on?
It is precisely as I have stated.
Paul presents an impossible proposition, implying that since they are devoid of love, they do not really possess those gifts, but merely assume the name and appearance.
And in order to strip them of those gifts, he grants for the sake of argument that they are what in reality they are not.
Text: 1 John 3:13-18.
13 Do not marvel, brothers, if the world hates you.
14 We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers.
Whoever does not love abides in death.
15 Anyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in him.
16 By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
17 But whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, and shuts off his compassion from him, how does the love of God abide in him?
18 My little children, let us not love in word, nor with the tongue, but in deed and truth.
1. The Epistles and Gospels chosen for the Sundays of the Pentecost season have love as their general theme.

They deal not only with the love we owe to Christ and God, which is simply to be thankful for the unspeakable blessing of the forgiveness of sins and salvation through Christ’s blood and death, but also with the love we owe our neighbor—not a love given in return for favors, but one that unceasingly gives, forgives, and does every good even when it is not returned.
2. John here urges the Christian to practice the virtue of love.
Considering how plainly rare love is among men, this admonition is necessary.
He especially warns Christians not to wonder at the world’s hatred and its desire for their death.
Such was the hatred of Cain for his brother, of which the apostle has just spoken.
The world’s hatred, it must be admitted, repels love and powerfully hinders its exercise.
3. Is it not exceedingly strange that anyone can hate those who love him and from whom he has received nothing but kindness?
Such wickedness is almost inconceivable, we say.
What incentive does anyone have to serve the world when, in its ingratitude, it repays love with hatred?
But let us examine ourselves, who are baptized and have received the Gospel, and confess how we repay the supreme love of God in giving us his Son.
What a beautiful example of glad gratitude we display!
For the shame of it we ought to despise ourselves before God and his angels.

And what shall we say of those who will not endure the preaching of the glorious message of God’s grace and blessing, but condemn it as heresy? To them, those who seek to serve, benefit, and save the world by proclaiming the good news must be, as Paul says, “as the filth of the world, the scum of all things” (1 Corinthians 4:13).
Indeed, no criminal receives more wretched and shameful treatment and execution, of which the Pope and his followers are a case in point.

blocks.x: The World’s Hatred.

s: 4. Although experience has proven this otherwise incredible fact, John still sees fit to give the admonition: “Do not marvel, brothers, if the world hates you.”
If we are not to wonder at this, is there anything in the world that should stir wonder?
I would truly think that hearing a single sermon on the grace of Christ would be enough to bring the world to receive the Gospel with intense joy and never to forget the divine mercy and blessing.

It would be no wonder if the earth suddenly opened and swallowed mankind because of its ingratitude to God, who has given his Son to become man in order to redeem us condemned mortals from sin and death and to restore us to life and salvation.
Is it not a horrible thing that anyone should shun and oppose such a Savior and his doctrine even more than he does the devil himself?
5. But what is God’s attitude toward such conduct?
Well does he say to the Jews through the prophet: “O my people, what have I done to you? And how have I wearied you? Bear witness against me.
For I brought you up out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of bondage; and I sent Moses, Aaron, and Miriam before you.
O my people, remember now what Balak king of Moab plotted, and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him; remember from Shittim to Gilgal, so that you may know the righteous acts of Jehovah.”

Micah 6:3-5. And well does Christ say to his ungrateful people: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to her! How often would I have gathered your children together, even as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not!”
Matthew 23:37. As if he would say, “I surely did not come to bring about your death and condemnation by my message.
I am about to suffer death and God’s wrath for your sins.
I bring you God’s endless grace and blessing for time and eternity.
Then why this bitter hatred against me and my message?”
6. “Since the world hates even God for his kindness,” John argues, “do not marvel, my beloved, that you suffer the same fate.
What does it matter that I show my love by risking life and limb to uphold this doctrine of the Gospel and to help my neighbor?
Mine is but a poor, mean, crude, offensive love compared with the love that led Christ to die for me and to redeem me from eternal death.
If God’s supreme, unfathomable love fails to awaken the gratitude of the world, what wonder is it if the world hates you for all your kindness?
Why will you bring down your fist and stamp your foot in anger at such ingratitude?
You yourselves are of that race for whom the Son of God had to die.

And even if you were to die for the Gospel, your sacrifice would be as nothing compared to the fact that God, for the sake of the world, did not spare his own Son but allowed the world to put him to death.”
7. But where does the world’s hatred come from?
John tells us in verse twelve, when he mentions the incident of Cain, who, he says, “was of the evil one and killed his brother.
And why did he kill him?
Because his works were evil, and his brother’s righteous.”
An excellent reason for hating, indeed—the hater and murderer is evil and the benefactor good!
In civil and domestic affairs it is the evildoers and the disobedient who incur displeasure and receive punishment; and such a reward is just.
But whenever God has dealings with the world, it shows what a rotten fruit it is by hating, persecuting, and putting to death its very benefactors as evildoers and impostors.
This trait it inherits, John tells us, from its ancestor Cain, the great fratricide saint.
He is a true picture of the world of all times, and its spirit and fashion are ever patterned after him.

8. When mother Eve, the dear, godly woman, bore her first son, she declared in her joy and in her hope of God’s promise of the future seed that would bruise the serpent’s head: “I have gotten a man with the help of Jehovah” (Genesis 4:1); and she named him Cain, which means “obtained,” as if she would say, “I have obtained the true treasure.”
For she had never before seen a human being born; this was the first, precious fruit of mankind.
Over Cain she rejoiced, pronouncing herself blessed.
This son was brought up in the hope that he would be a savior of the future race, a comfort to his brothers and sisters and all their offspring.
Nor was he unaware of these proud hopes.

Proudly he lorded it over his brother, who by contrast had to bear the shameful name of Abel, meaning “nothing,” or “vanity,” as if voicing the thought of the parents’ hearts: “Alas! This one has no future.
Cain is the rightful heir to the blessing God has promised man; he is lord and master of his brothers.”

9. It is likely that the godly father and mother for many years drew their comfort from the hope they placed in their first-born son, as they looked forward with the most intense longing to redemption from their deplorable fall.

No doubt they trained both sons very carefully and instructed them concerning their own sin and fall and the promise God had given them, until the sons were fully grown and had entered into the priestly office.

Cain the first-born was particularly zealous in this respect, wanting to be first, inasmuch as he offered his first fruits of the earth, given by God and obtained by his own labor, as he had no doubt seen his father offer.
Abel, however, the lesser one, the poor shepherd, offered the firstlings of his sheep, given him by God and obtained without effort and toil of his own.
Now God, in a wonderful way, showed his preference concerning the gifts upon the altar.
Fire came down from heaven and consumed Abel’s offering, but Cain’s remained.
The fire was the sign of God’s favor.
The text says: “And Jehovah had respect for Abel and for his offering, but for Cain and for his offering he had no respect.”
Genesis 4:4-5.
10. Then Adam and Eve saw that the hope and comfort they had centered in their first-born son were a delusion.
They began to learn the wonderful judgments of God, who gave precedence to Abel, the male counterpart of Cinderella—which is all he was in his own eyes when he compared himself with his brother.
Now Cain, fully confident in his position and spoiled by his parents’ delusion that as the first-born he was God’s favorite, felt himself outraged.
His hypocrisy, masked until now, comes to the surface.
He burns with secret hatred against God, and with hatred and anger against his brother, which he takes no trouble whatever to hide.
His parents rebuke him, but accomplish nothing.
The flame of his resentment rises higher, and meeting his brother alone in the field, he strikes him to the ground.
Far from considering amendment of life or seeking grace from God, he has no mercy on the only brother he has on earth, who has done him no harm whatever.
He cannot forgive him and leave him in unenvied possession of the grace of God.
11. Such was the comfort and joy poor Adam and Eve lived to experience in their first children!

From this time on their earthly life was filled with gloom and sorrow, especially since they could not help but see the source of these in their own fall; and they would have pined away to death had not God comforted them with another son.

For when it became evident that the hope they had placed in Cain was a delusion, and that they had been deprived of the son who, beyond a doubt, possessed the grace of God, they, without another son, would not have known where to look for the comfort of the promised seed.

blocks.x: Cain the World, Abel the Church.

s: 12. Note that in this man Cain the world is pictured in its true, characteristic colors; in him its true spirit stands reflected.
Certainly his equal has never existed.
In him are unquestionably prefigured the very flower, the very essence, of holiness on earth—the most pious servants of God.
On the other hand, that poor, wretched, lowly male counterpart of Cinderella, Abel, well represents the obscure little brotherhood, the Church of Christ.
She must yield to Cain the lord the distinction of being everything before God, of receiving every gift of God, of being entitled to all honor and every privilege.
He feels important in his imagined dignity, lets this spirit pervade his sacrifices and his worship, and thinks that God cannot help but favor and accept his offering rather than his brother’s.
Meanwhile, the pious Abel goes his way, meekly enduring his brother’s contempt.
He willingly yields the honor to Cain, considers himself far inferior, and sees no comfort for himself apart from the pure mercy and goodness of God.
He believes in God and hopes for the promised future seed.
In such faith he performs his sacrifice as a confession, a sign, of his gratitude.

13. This illustration is intended by God as comfort for his little band; for the incident is not written for Abel’s sake but for the sake of the humble children of God, whose condition is like Abel’s.
God has not forgotten them, though they are haughtily ignored by proud Cain, who regards them as nothing in his presence.
God graciously looks upon them and rejects proud Cain with his birthright and offering.

14. Innocent Abel becomes the object of anger and hatred when the Word of God takes hold of Cain, revealing God’s displeasure where Cain had imagined himself worthy, and God’s unwillingness to regard his offering and devotion as superior to his brother’s and more meritorious.
Cain begins to hate and persecute his brother bitterly.
He finds no rest until Abel is struck down and cut off from the earth.
Now you have the cause of the world’s hatred and anger against Christians; it is simply this, as John says of Cain: “Because his works were evil, and his brother’s righteous.”
15. What offense had godly Abel committed against his brother to be so hated?
He had even regarded that brother as the first-born, as far superior to himself, and had shown him every honor and loved him as a brother should.
He was easily satisfied, desiring only the grace of God.
He prayed for the future seed, that is, for the salvation and happiness of his parents, his brother, and the entire human race.
How could Cain be so unmerciful and inhuman in his frenzy as to murder his own flesh and blood?
The answer lies in the fact that the devil had filled Cain’s heart with pride and vanity over his birthright.
He considered himself a man of distinction, with every claim upon God’s favor, and sinless, while his brother was nothing whatever.
Cain’s heart is empty of true brotherly love; he has only contempt for Abel.
He cannot endure God’s evident favor toward his brother, and will not be moved by the command to humble himself and seek God’s grace.
Anger and envy possess him to such an extent that he cannot bear to let his brother live.
In violation of God’s commandment and his own conscience, he becomes a murderer, and then goes his way as if he had done right.
16. This is what John means when he says that Cain had no other cause for his crime than that his own works were evil and his brother’s righteous.
In the same way that obedient daughter of Saint Cain, the world, hates the Christians—and for no other reason than their love and goodness of heart.
Witness the examples of the holy patriarchs, the prophets, and, most of all, Christ himself.
17. What sin against the world did the beloved apostles commit?
They desired no one’s injury, but went about in extreme poverty and toil, teaching mankind how to be saved, through faith in Christ, from the devil’s kingdom and from eternal death.
This the world will not hear or tolerate; hence the hue and cry: “Kill, kill these people!
Away with them from the earth!
Show them no mercy!”
Why this hostility? Because the apostles sought to free the world from its idolatry and damnable doings.
Such good works the world could not tolerate.
What it desires is nothing but praise and commendation for its own evil doings, expecting from God the impossible endorsement: “Your deeds are good and well-pleasing to me.
You are pious children of mine.
Just keep on cheerfully killing all who believe and preach my Word.”
18. In the same way the world conducts itself today toward our Gospel.

We are hated and persecuted for no other reason than that we have, by God’s grace, proclaimed his Word, which rescued us from the blindness and idolatry in which we were sunk as deeply as the world, and because we desire to rescue others.
That is the unpardonable sin by which we have incurred the world’s irreconcilable anger and its inextinguishable hatred.
It cannot allow us to live.
We preach no other doctrine than faith in Christ, which our children pray and which they themselves confess in words.
We differ only in our claim that, since Christ was crucified for us and shed his blood to redeem us from sin and death, our salvation is not accomplished by our own works, or holiness, or devotion.

The fact that we do not regard their faithless worship as equal to Christ himself, but teach men to trust in the grace of God and not in their own worthiness, and to render him gratitude for his grace—this fact is intolerable to the world.

It would be well for our adversaries if they would receive such teaching, since it would make them more than ever what they profess to be: our superiors in wisdom, knowledge, and reputation—a claim we are willing to concede.
But Cain’s works are evil and Abel’s righteous.
The world simply cannot tolerate the Gospel, and no unity or harmony is ever to be hoped for.
The world will not forsake its idolatry nor receive the faith.
It would force us either to renounce the Word of God and praise its Cain-like worship, or to accept death at their hands.
19. Therefore John says, “Do not marvel, brothers, if the world hates you,” for it is compelled to act according to the nature it has inherited from its father Cain.
It would have all the merit and grant Abel none.
The world consists of the exalted, the wise, the learned, the mighty.
The Scriptures represent these as bound by necessity to hate and persecute the poor band of the Church of Christ because of the good works done by them.
Under no circumstances can they tolerate the idea of being taught by this despised and humble band the doctrine of salvation through the grace and mercy of God alone, not through man’s own merits.
They cannot endure the teaching that their offering—the Mass, regarded by the Papists as a work of supreme merit and holiness—avails nothing before God.
20. In the text the nature of the world is portrayed so that we may recognize it.
To understand the world well enough to know what may be expected from it is essential and valuable knowledge for the Christian.
Armed in this way, he will not be dismayed and become impatient under suffering, nor allow its malice and ingratitude to mislead him into hatred and a desire for revenge.
He will keep his faith and love, letting the world go its way if it refuses to hear his message.
The Christian should expect nothing better from the world than its bitter persecution in return for his good works and love.
Let him remember that the Church of Christ on earth is never to have an easier lot.

He is not to judge by show and appearance, thinking: “They are the great multitude, the wisest and cleverest people on earth; how is it possible that they should all be in error and under condemnation?”
21. It is necessarily true that discipline and peace are impossible without the most excellent, exalted, learned, clever people—royal, princely, noble in achievement and honor.
Cain is never plain and lowly.
He is always eminently clever, wise, holy, and in every way vastly superior to Abel.
In fact, he must in himself represent all desirable things, as his name indicates.

And the same characteristic is evident in his children, who are ingenious in inventing every kind of art. Deplorable is the fact that a man of Cain’s qualifications, born of godly parents and signally honored by God, should display such hatred and inhumanity toward poor Abel merely because of God’s Word and Abel’s faith.

22. Such knowledge is comforting to the godly little company of Christians, who are confident that they have God’s favor and know it to be the occasion of their persecution; they have no protection or help but are exposed to the same fate as Abel.
If they fare better, they may thank God for it.
But they are always to abide in love toward God, whose love they have received and felt, and likewise toward men, their enemies not excepted.
This was Abel’s way; could he have lived again, he would have kept his brotherly love for his murderer, forgiving him and even pleading for God’s forgiveness for him.
“We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers.”

blocks.x: Love Moves Christians.

s: 23. To abide in love should be the motive for us Christians.
John contrasts it with the motive of the world in hating us—its wickedness.
The world’s hatred of you, as John’s words imply, is not strange.
The contrast between you and the world is exceedingly great.
Through its own evil works, unbelief, pride, contempt for the Word and grace of God, and persecution of the godly, the world has by this time become the victim of Satan and eternal death.
It spurns all counsel and help aimed at its rescue.
Stiff-necked and hardened, evidently condemned by its own conscience, it has chosen to persist in its doom.
But we believers in Christ, God be praised, are different people!
We have come forth from death; we have passed through death and entered into life through the knowledge and faith of the Son of God, who has loved us and given himself for us.

24. Such grace and goodness of God, says the apostle, should move you not to be offended and overcome by the world’s ingratitude, hatred, and malice, and so to cease from holy endeavor and likewise become evil—a course that will result in the loss of your treasure.
It is yours not by your own effort but by grace alone; for at one time you, as well as they, languished in the kingdom and power of death, in evil works, far from faith and love.
Remember, therefore, to comfort yourselves with the thought of this great blessing, an advantage you enjoy above the others.
What if the world, abiding in death, does hate and persecute you who abide in life?
Whom can its hatred injure?
It cannot take from you the life it lacks while you possess it, nor deliver you to death, from which you have passed through Christ.

When it does its worst, it may perhaps falsely slander you, or deprive you of your property, or destroy your corrupt body—the final home of maggots and in any event doomed to decay—and so, through the death of the body, help you gain true life.
Thus the vengeance will be yours rather than its own.
Yours will be the joy of being transplanted from death into life, while the world must abide in death.
While those of the world think to deny you both the kingdom of heaven and the kingdom of earth, they themselves lose body and soul.
What more terrible retribution could their hatred and envy receive?

In order not to give the devil and the world that satisfaction, and much more for your own welfare, you must not allow your persecutions to rob you of your peace and salvation, nor lead you to lose your faith through impatience and desire for revenge.
Rather, pity their wretchedness and doom.
You lose nothing by their oppression; yours is the gain, theirs the loss.
For the slight grief inflicted on you in body and in time, it shall pay dearly both here and hereafter.
25. How do we know that we have passed from death into life?
John says: because we love the brothers.
Just what does he mean?
Is it not our doctrine that Christ first loved us, as John says elsewhere? That before we ever loved him he died and rose again for us?
When we fully believe in our Savior’s love, then our own hearts respond with perfect love to God and our neighbor.
Why, then, does John say, “We have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers”?
26. The explanation is found in the words “We know.”
John says plainly, “From the fact that we love the brothers, we know that we have passed out of death into life.”
Love of the brothers is the test by which we may determine who are the true believers.
The apostle directed this epistle especially against false Christians; there are many who extol Christ, as unbelieving Cain did, and yet fail to bear the fruit of faith.
John is referring not to the means by which we pass from sin and death to life, but to the proof by which we may know the fact—not to the cause, but to the effect.
27. It is not enough to boast of having passed from death into life; there must be evidence of the fact.
Faith is not an idle and lifeless thing.
When there is faith in the heart, its power will be evident.
Where power is not in evidence, all boasting is false and vain.

When the human heart, in its confidence in divine mercy and love, is thrilled with spiritual comfort and also warmed into kindness, friendliness, humility, and patience toward the neighbor, envying and despising no one but cheerfully serving all and ministering to their need, even to the point of risking body and life—when this is the case, then the fruits of faith are evident.
Such fruits are proof that the believer has truly passed from death into life.
If he did not have true faith, but doubted God’s grace and love, his heart would not move him, out of love and gratitude to God, to show love for his neighbor.

Where a man has faith, and where he realizes God’s infinite mercy and goodness in raising him from death to life, love is kindled in his heart, and he is moved to do every kind of good, even to his enemies, as God has done to him.
28. Such is the right interpretation and understanding of John’s expression: “We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers.”
It leaves the foundation intact—justification, or deliverance from death, through faith alone.
This is the first element of Christian doctrine.
Granting that faith does justify, the next question is whether the faith is real or feigned, being merely a deceptive show and an unsupported claim.

The clear teaching given by the apostles is that love, indeed, does not deliver from death, but that deliverance from death and the presence of life become a matter of sight and knowledge in that love has been produced.

With true faith we must have come to the point where we no longer, like Cain, in our pride and conceit, despise our neighbor; where we are not filled with envy, hatred, and bitterness; where we desire, and to the extent of our power promote, the interests of our neighbor and do him every good.
