29. John draws to a close by showing the opposite side of the picture, in that he addresses earnest words that echo like peals of thunder to those who make the carnal boast of being Christians while lacking love.
He cites several facts as evidence that where love is lacking, faith and deliverance from death are necessarily absent as well.
In this way no opportunity is left for self-deception or for a frivolous excuse based on wordy boasting of one’s faith.
The reality of the inner life is known by the presence of love, which in turn attests the presence of faith in the heart.
I. “Whoever does not love abides in death.”
30. Here, in clear, decisive words, the conclusion is stated that no one may boast of life unless he has love.

If it is true that faith must be active, it is conversely true that the absence of fruit demonstrates that one continues in the old Cain-like manner of existence, sluggish and dead, bereft of comfort and of the experience of God’s grace and life.
Let no one presume to think he has passed into life as long as he is without love and the fruits of faith.
Let him become serious and, in alarm, make ready to become a true believer, lest he remain in eternal death and under greater condemnation than those who have never heard the Gospel.
II. “Anyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in him.”
31. Still clearer and stronger becomes the argument that lack of love means continuing in death.
The stern and frightful judgment is here expressed that the unloving person is no better than Cain the fratricide.
His heart is under the sway of deadly hatred and murderous malice against the brother who refuses to be subservient to his desires.
His kindling rage will prove its existence by corresponding works unless it is restrained by fear of disgrace and punishment.
He wishes his brother nothing good, but rejoices in his misfortune.
All this, however, is impossible for one who believes that he has been delivered from death.

One who knows from experience the wretchedness and misery of death, but has entered into life with its comfort and joy—blessings he seeks to keep—such a person will desire the same blessing for others; he cannot rejoice in another’s death.
Therefore the converse is true: “We know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in him.”

blocks.x: Hatred Natural to Human Reason.

s: 32. Thus we see the nature of the human heart without faith and the knowledge of Christ; at bottom it is but the heart of a Cain, murderous toward its neighbor.
Nor can anything better be expected from one who is not a Christian.
The Scriptures repeatedly denounce such faithless hypocrites as bloodthirsty and deceitful.
“Jehovah abhors the bloodthirsty and deceitful man.”
Psalm 5:6. “For their feet run to evil, and they hurry to shed blood.”
Proverbs 1:16. See also verse 11.
All mankind are by nature the children of the murderer Cain.
They are, of course, no better than their father.

Though Cain was a most magnificent, intelligent, and wise man, being the first fruit born of those holy parents Adam and Eve, and in his superior endowment with natural virtues infinitely superior to all who came after him, he was nevertheless an unbeliever before God.
Hence he became the murderer of his brother.
III. “By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
But whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, and shuts off his compassion from him, how does the love of God abide in him?”
33. These words portray true Christian love and hold up the sublime example, or pattern, of God’s love revealed in Christ.
Christ’s blood and death are God’s own blood and death.
Paul, in Acts 20:28, speaks of God having purchased the Church “with his own blood.”
The heart of man by faith receives and grasps this sacrifice.
Under its transforming influence he is inclined to do good to his neighbor as he himself has received good.
He even risks his life to that end, being conscious of his redemption from eternal death and knowing that physical death is powerless to affect his eternal life.
But the heart that fails to take hold of Christ’s sacrifice is without faith and insensible to God’s love and eternal life.
34. John uses an illustration plain enough for anyone to understand, and from which we may judge that the soul found wanting in small duties will be deficient in great ones.

According to the apostle, if someone possesses this world’s goods and sees his neighbor in want, being able to help without harm to himself, and yet closes his heart against that neighbor, not helping him with even the slightest work of love, how can the love of God dwell in him, since he values it so little that he will not spare his needy brother a penny?
How can he be expected, then, to render a greater service—even to lay down his life for his brother?
What right has such a soul to boast—how can he know—that Christ has laid down his life for him and delivered him from death?
35. How often such people are to be found!
Having this world’s goods and being able to help the needy, they close their hearts against the unfortunate, as the rich glutton did toward poor Lazarus.

Where shall we find in imperial courts, among kings, princes, and lords, any who extend a helping hand to the needy Church, or give her so much as a crust of bread toward the support of the poor, of the ministry, and of schools, or for any other of her needs?
How would they measure up in the greater duty of laying down their lives for the brothers, and especially for the Christian Church?
Note the terrible judgment that those who lack brotherly love are murderers in God’s sight and cannot have eternal life.

36. But the merely selfish may well escape our censure in comparison with those who not only close their purses to the poor but shamelessly and forcibly deprive and rob their needy neighbor of what is his by overreaching, fraud, oppression, and extortion; who take from the Church the property rightfully hers and especially set apart for her, snatching the bread from her mouth, so to speak.

Not only is the papist rabble today guilty of such sin, but many who would be known as evangelical practice the same fraud with regard to the parish estates and general property of the Church, and in addition tyrannically harass and torment the poor ministers.
But oh, how heavy and terrible is the judgment awaiting those who have denied Christ the Lord in his thirst even a cup of cold water!
IV. “My little children, let us not love in word, nor with the tongue, but in deed and truth.”
37. The world and the false Christians pretend great love in word; but in practice, when love should show itself in deeds, it is found to be insincere.

So John admonishes that where our love is not ardent enough to lead us to lay down our lives for our brothers, however much we may profess Christ, that love is surely only a vain show, a false pretense, by which we deceive ourselves and remain in unbelief and death, and in a more deplorable condition than those who are wholly ignorant of the Gospel.
Therefore let whoever would proceed safely and prove himself a Christian remember to prove himself such by his deeds and works.
Then men will know that he does not follow the devil like others, as a murderer and liar.
They will know, on the contrary, that he truly and with his heart clings to the Word of God, having passed from death to life.
